Wings: Moderately short (approximately 10–12 cm in length), with rounded wingtips and a dark brownish-black primary flight feathers. The secondary coverts are pale grayish-brown, and the entire wing profile is relatively compact.  
Tail: Long (approximately 10–12 cm), graduated with a distinct black upper tail coverts and white under tail coverts. The tail exhibits a slight upward curve and is relatively stiff, with the upper tail coverts forming a dark, narrow band across the tail base.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brownish-black in color, slender with sharp, pointed claws. Feet are non-webbed, typical of flycatchers, with a short, robust tarsus and three toes (hallux) adapted for perching.

Body Size: Approximately 10–11 cm in length (excluding tail), with a compact, slightly rounded head and a proportionally short neck. Significantly smaller than conspecifics of the genus *Muscicapa* (e.g., *M. warreni*), exhibiting a dense, compact body outline with minimal visible subcutaneous tissue.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a pale, uniform brownish-gray body with fine, dark brown streaking on the flanks and undertail coverts. Feather texture is soft and fine, with short barbules and minimal downy covering. Juveniles are duller, showing a more olive-brown hue with less defined streaking and a slightly paler overall tone compared to adults.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved; color is dark brown with a pale yellowish tip. Length is approximately 10–12 mm, and the tip is fine and slightly chisel-like without significant webbing.  
Eyes: Iris color is a uniform, pale brown (not distinctly reddish or blue).  
Face: Periorbital area is pale brown with fine, dark brown streaking; base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no distinct facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-brown with fine, dark brown streaking; texture is soft and smooth without significant downy covering.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a slight upcurved tip; primary feathers are pale brown with dark brown tips, and secondary feathers are uniformly pale brown. Wing length is approximately 50–55% of total body length.  
Tail: Short, graduated tail (approximately 40–45% of body length); upper tail coverts are dark brown with pale brown edges, while under tail coverts are pale brown with fine dark streaking. Tail shape is slightly flattened and stiff.  
Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown legs with sharp, pointed claws; feet are non-webbed and adapted for perching on small branches.

Body Size: 12–14 cm in length; compact and relatively slender build with a slightly rounded head profile, smaller than the Black-capped Flycatcher (*Empidonax niger*) but comparable in size to the Eastern Phoebe (*Sayornis phoeo*). Overall outline is short, with a proportionally large head and a moderately short neck.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform olive-brown upper body with fine, soft downy texture; underparts are pale grayish-white with subtle brownish streaking on the flanks. Juveniles are duller, with a more brownish-gray back, less defined streaking on the underparts, and a fainter buffish tinge to the throat. The plumage is relatively dense with short, fine feathers, lacking the pronounced glossiness of some other flycatcher species.  
Beak: Short, slightly decurved, and robust with a dark grayish-black coloration; tip is blunt and slightly chisel-like, measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length. Not notably stout compared to other *Empidonax* species.  
Eyes: Iris is a uniform brown color, lacking the green or yellow hues seen in some flycatchers.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale buff with a subtle, narrow band of pale grayish-brown extending from the base of the bill to the cheek; base of the beak is dark grayish-black, and there are no distinct facial patches or markings beyond the periorbital buff band.  
Abdomen: Whitish with faint, irregular brownish streaking; texture is soft and fine, typical of flycatcher underparts.  
Wings: Moderately long (approximately 100–110 mm), with rounded wingtips and a distinct dark brownish-black coloration on the coverts and primaries; secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown with dark edges, creating a subtle contrast against the olive-brown back.  
Tail: Relatively long (approximately 60–70% of body length), with a graduated tapering shape; upper tail coverts are olive-brown with pale edges, while under tail coverts are white with dark brownish tips.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown coloration; slender and relatively short, with sharp, non-webbed claws (typical of flycatchers).

Body Size: Approximately 15–17 cm in length (excluding tail), with a slender, elongated body outline and a relatively short neck compared to conspecifics like the Black-capped Flycatcher (*Melaenornis*). The overall form is compact yet agile, with a lightweight build suited for rapid flight and perch-hopping.

Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform olive-brown upper body with fine, subtle barring on the flanks; the underparts are pale yellowish-white with faint, irregular brownish barring. Feather texture is soft and slightly glossy, not fluffy. Juveniles are duller, with less distinct barring, a more olive-brown hue, and a pale buffish throat, gradually developing adult plumage over 1–2 years.

Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved (curved downward at the tip), measuring 10–12 mm in length. Color is dark grayish-brown with a pale base; the tip is blunt, not hooked, consistent with flycatcher feeding adaptations.

Eyes: Iris color is dark brown, lacking prominent eye-ring or contrasting markings.

Face: Periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale yellowish-white with a narrow, faintly defined pale stripe. The base of the beak is dark grayish-brown, and there are no distinct facial patches or markings.

Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with fine, irregular brownish barring; texture is soft and slightly velvety, not glossy.

Wings: Short, rounded wings with a slight taper; primary feathers are long but not prominently visible. Coverts are dark brown, with a pale buffish base on the secondary feathers.

Tail: Exceptionally long (10–12 cm), forming a distinctive "scissor" shape due to the elongated central tail feathers (rectrices) that extend beyond the wings. Upper tail coverts are dark brown with pale tips, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white with dark brownish edges.

Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown in color; feet are slender with sharp, pointed claws (no webbing), typical of arboreal passerines.

Body Size: Small to medium-sized flycatcher (12–14 cm in length), with a compact, streamlined body outline. Slightly smaller and more slender than *Empidonatus* flycatchers of similar habitat; overall proportions exhibit a short, relatively heavy head and a moderately long neck for its size.  
Body Plumage: Males display a vivid vermilion (deep red) head, nape, and throat, contrasting with a pale olive-brown back and wings. Females are olive-brown with subtle streaking on the flanks and pale underparts. Juveniles are duller, with pale brownish-gray upperparts, faint streaking, and a pale buff throat lacking the male's intense red; plumage texture is fine, slightly glossy, and non-velvety.  
Beak: Short, slender, and sharply pointed; color is black with a distinct, subtle hook at the tip (adapted for gleaning insects). Length is approximately 12 mm, with moderate stoutness relative to body size.  
Eyes: Iris is uniformly dark brown, lacking any contrasting hues.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale buff with a distinct pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head. Base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches beyond the pale periorbital stripe.  
Abdomen: White to pale yellowish-white in males (slightly more yellow in summer), smooth and unmarked; females are pale buff with faint, irregular streaking. Texture is soft and non-ribbed.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a slight taper; length is approximately 60% of body length. Primary feathers are dark brown, with secondary feathers pale brown and narrowly tipped in black.  
Tail: Moderately long (12–15 mm), graduated with a distinct central pair of tail feathers; upper tail coverts are vermilion in males (pale brown in females), while under tail coverts are white with a faint brownish tinge.  
Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown in color; feet are non-webbed with sharp, pointed claws (adapted for perching on branches).

Body Size: Small to medium-sized flycatcher (10–11 cm in length), slender and agile build with a relatively short neck; slightly smaller than conspecific *Empidonax* species like the Eastern Flycatcher (12–13 cm) and less robust than *Mimus* species. Overall outline is compact with a distinct head-to-body ratio favoring maneuverability in dense foliage.  
Body Plumage: Olive-brown upperparts with fine vellus texture; pale yellowish-white underparts (abdomen and ventral flank), fading to whitish on the chest; juveniles exhibit duller, more brownish-gray upperparts and a faintly olive-brown wash on the flanks, with less pronounced yellowing on the belly compared to adults.  
Beak: Dark grayish-black in color, short, slender, and moderately hooked at the tip (approximately 12–15 mm in length), with a fine, sharp apex for insect capture.  
Eyes: Iris color is medium brown (not green or blue), with a subtle golden sheen in optimal light.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellowish-white with a distinct dark brown eye stripe; base of the beak is pale yellow, lacking any contrasting patches or markings.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with a faint, irregular brownish tinge along the midline; texture is soft and non-velvety, with minimal downy covering.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings (approximately 60% of body length) with a slight curve; flight feathers are pale brown with dark brown tips, and secondary coverts are pale grayish-brown.  
Tail: Long (approximately 100–120% of body length), graduated with a stiff, slightly flattened shape; upper tail coverts are dark brown with pale brown edges, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white with a faint brownish tinge.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender with sharp, pointed claws; feet are non-webbed, typical for terrestrial insectivores.

Body Size: The male Augustus frigatebird (Fregata magnificens) attains a body length of 60–70 cm (24–28 in) with a wingspan exceeding 1.5 m (5 ft). It exhibits a slender, streamlined body outline characteristic of frigatebirds, significantly smaller than the closely related sooty frigatebird (Fregata martens) but proportionally more robust than the lesser frigatebird (Fregata ariel) in the same ecological niche. This size facilitates exceptional aerial agility and long-distance soaring.

Body Plumage: Adults display a vivid crimson to deep red plumage on the upper breast and chest, transitioning to a pale, almost whitish base on the lower chest and abdomen. The plumage is smooth and glossy, with fine, interlocking barbules typical of frigatebirds. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale streaking on the flanks and a dull, unmarked head, lacking the vivid red coloration and exhibiting a more matte texture compared to the glossy, iridescent adult plumage.

Beak: The beak is long, slender, and sharply recurved with a distinct, pointed tip. It is predominantly black in color, with a pale, almost ivory base on the lower mandible that becomes progressively darker toward the tip. The beak is not webbed, consistent with its specialized aerial foraging behavior.

Eyes: The iris is a deep, uniform brown, lacking any distinct color variation or reflective properties.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale, almost whitish, forming a distinct eye patch that contrasts sharply with the dark beak base. The base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches beyond the pale eye region.

Abdomen: The abdomen is predominantly white with a faint, pale brownish tinge along the ventral margin. The texture is smooth and unfeathered in the central region, typical of frigatebirds.

Wings: The wings are exceptionally long (exceeding 1.5 m) and narrow, with a pointed, angular shape. The primary feathers are dark brown to black, while the secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown with a subtle, pale terminal band. The wings are held in a characteristic "V" shape during flight.

Tail: The tail is short (approximately 15–20 cm) and relatively stiff, with dark brown upper tail coverts and pale white under tail coverts. The tail lacks a distinct central pair of feathers and is generally held relatively flat during flight.

Legs and Feet: The legs are slender and relatively short, with sharp, pointed claws. The feet are unwebbed and adapted for perching on low vegetation or rocks, not for swimming or aquatic locomotion. The coloration is dark brown to black.

Body Size: Medium-sized seabird (45–50 cm in length), slightly larger than the common puffin but smaller than the herring gull. Streamlined, elongated body with a relatively short neck and robust thorax, presenting a compact, aerodynamic outline typical of pelagic species.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a predominantly white body with a dark grayish-brown back, wings, and tail coverts; plumage is dense, slightly stiff, and water-resistant. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale streaking on the flanks and a distinct pale rump patch, fading to near-white in subsequent years.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, moderately stout with a pronounced, slightly curved tip (approximately 30–40 mm in length), and a sharp, chisel-like edge adapted for scraping food from rocky substrates.  
Eyes: Iris is dark brown to black in adults.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white with a distinct dark brown eye patch; base of the beak is dark gray, and no specialized facial patches are present.  
Abdomen: Pale white with a subtle yellowish tinge in some individuals; texture is smooth and slightly glossy.  
Wings: Moderately long (150–170 mm), narrow and pointed with dark brown leading edges and pale white trailing edges; primary feathers are dark gray, while secondary feathers are pale brown with white tips.  
Tail: Short (approx. 100 mm), rounded in shape; upper tail coverts are dark brown with pale white tips, while under tail coverts are pale white with dark brown margins.  
Legs and Feet: Dark gray to black in color; legs are moderately slender with slightly webbed feet (reduced webbing) and sharp, curved claws adapted for gripping rocky surfaces.

Body Size: Medium-sized dabbling duck (45–52 cm in length), slightly smaller than Mallard but larger than Pintail; compact, somewhat rounded body outline with a relatively short neck and broad chest.
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform olive-brown upperparts with a distinct dark brownish head and neck, soft dense plumage; juveniles are pale brownish-gray with faint white patches on the cheeks and a duller overall appearance, lacking the defined head pattern of adults.
Beak: Dark gray to black, moderately long, slightly decurved, with a sharp, pointed tip and minimal visible keratin flaking.
Eyes: Dark brown iris.
Face: Pale buff periorbital area, dark brown base of the beak, no distinct facial patches or markings.
Abdomen: White with fine, inconspicuous brownish streaks in adults; clean white in juveniles without streaking.
Wings: Moderately long, broad with dark brown coverts, flight feathers dark gray to black; secondary coverts show subtle olive-brown tones.
Tail: Short (10–12 cm), rounded; upper tail coverts olive-brown, under tail coverts white with faint brownish edges.

Body Size: The American Goldfinch (*Spinus tristis*) measures 10–11 cm in body length (excluding tail) and possesses a compact, rounded body outline with a relatively short neck and a proportionally large head. It is slightly smaller than the House Sparrow (*Passer domesticus*) but larger than the House Finch (*Haemorhous mexicanus*), with a body mass of approximately 12–15 grams.

Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a strikingly vivid yellow plumage on the upperparts and underparts, with a black cap and a black eye stripe. The feathers are fine, soft, and densely packed, creating a velvety texture. Juveniles are distinctly different, displaying a pale olive-green head and upperparts with a faint brownish tinge, pale yellow underparts, and a lack of the adult's black markings; their plumage is less saturated and more uniformly dull compared to adults. The overall coloration is highly variable by season and sex, but males are intensely yellow with black accents, while females are more olive-brown.

Beak: The beak is short, conical, and robustly built for seed processing, measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length. It is blackish in color with a slightly hooked tip, and the base is pale yellow. The beak is not webbed and is adapted for precise manipulation of small seeds.

Eyes: The iris is uniformly brown in color, with a subtle golden sheen in adult males due to the yellow plumage contrast. No distinct color variation is observed between sexes.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is characterized by a distinct black eye stripe that extends from the base of the bill to the side of the head. The base of the beak is pale yellow, and there are no additional specialized patches beyond the eye stripe.

Abdomen: The abdomen is uniformly pale yellow with a fine, soft texture, lacking distinct barring or streaking. It is slightly broader than the breast and transitions smoothly into the ventral feathers.

Wings: The wings are short and moderately rounded, with a length of approximately 50–60 mm. The primary feathers are black with a pale yellow tip, and the secondary feathers are yellow with black subterminal markings. The coverts (the feathers covering the base of the wings) are pale yellow with blackish edges.

Tail: The tail is short, measuring approximately 40–50% of body length, and is graduated (narrowing toward the tip). The upper tail coverts are black with pale yellow edges, while the under tail coverts are yellow. The tail exhibits a slight curve and is relatively stiff.

Legs and Feet: The legs are slender and dark brown in color, with sharp, pointed claws. The feet are non-webbed (digitigrade), typical of passerines, and adapted for perching on small branches. The tarsus (leg segment) is short and robust.

Body Size: 12–14 cm in length, with a compact, streamlined body outline. Slightly smaller and more robust than the American Goldfinch (*Spinus tristis*) but proportionally more slender than the House Finch (*Haemorhous mexicanus*); overall body mass is light for its size, facilitating agile flight in dense vegetation.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a vibrant, uniform yellowish-olive on the upperparts (head, back, rump) transitioning to a bright, glossy yellow on the underparts, with a distinct blackish patch at the base of the tail. Juveniles are duller, with olive-brown upperparts, pale yellowish-brown underparts, and a faint streaking on the flanks; plumage becomes intensely yellow with blackish tail tips in the second breeding season. Feather texture is smooth, glossy, and slightly stiff, with minimal downy covering on the body.  
Beak: Short, conical, and slightly curved (with a subtle hook at the tip), measuring 10–12 mm in length. The base is robust, and the tip is fine and slightly chisel-like, adapted for seed processing.  
Eyes: Dark brown irises, with minimal visible sclera.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellowish-brown, contrasting sharply with the dark brown eye-ring. The base of the beak is pale yellow, and there are no distinct facial patches; the face is relatively clean and unmarked.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with a slight olive tinge, smooth and non-iridescent texture; minimal downy covering.  
Wings: Moderately short (15–18 cm), with a rounded tip and a distinct blackish-brown band across the primary feathers. The secondary feathers are pale yellowish-brown, and the wing coverts are pale yellow with subtle blackish edges.  
Tail: Short (5–6 cm), with a slightly graduated shape. Upper tail coverts are pale yellow with blackish tips, while under tail coverts are pale yellow with distinct white tips. The tail is relatively stiff and shows minimal movement during flight.  
Legs and Feet: Slender, with pale yellowish-brown coloration; feet are non-webbed, with three toes (two forward, one backward) and a small, bare skin patch on the lower beak. The claws are sharp and slightly curved, typical of finches.

Body Size: Medium-sized grackle (25–28 cm in length), slightly larger than the common grackle (*Quiscalus quiscula*) but smaller than the mourning dove (*Dendragapus murinus*). Exhibits a streamlined, elongated body outline with a distinct tapering posterior region, contributing to its characteristic "boat tail" morphology.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a uniformly black plumage with a strong metallic sheen (iridescent blue-black under direct light), featuring subtle ultraviolet reflection on the head and neck. Feather texture is smooth and densely packed, with no significant downy covering. Juveniles are duller, exhibiting a brownish-grayish hue on the head and upper body with pale buffish streaks along the flanks, fading to a more uniform dark brown as they mature; plumage becomes progressively glossier and darker in adulthood.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, conical and moderately stout (approximately 18 mm in length), with a sharp, pointed tip and a slight curvature at the base. Not webbed; lacks a visible cere.  
Eyes: Iris is a deep, uniform brown (approaching black) with no visible distinct rings or markings.  
Face: Periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale grayish-white, forming a distinct pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head. The base of the beak is dark gray, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no white or yellow markings).  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-brown in color, with a slight sheen; texture is soft and non-pennaceous, lacking significant down or vellus hair.  
Wings: Moderately long (approximately 200 mm), with a broad, rounded shape and pointed primary feathers. Upperwing coverts are dark gray, while the secondary coverts and tertials are black; wingtips exhibit a pale, slightly buffish hue.  
Tail: Short (approximately 100 mm), distinctly shaped like a boat (tapered posteriorly with a narrow, flat base), with upper tail coverts black and sharply defined. Under tail coverts are pale yellowish-brown, contrasting with the dark upper tail coverts and providing a subtle visual cue for the "boat" shape.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with robust, slightly muscular structure; feet are unwebbed, featuring three toes (two forward, one backward) and sharp, pointed claws adapted for terrestrial movement.

Body Size: Approximately 25–28 cm in length (excluding tail), with a compact, streamlined body outline. Slightly smaller than the Great Grebe (*Podiceps major*) but larger than the Little Grebe (*Tachybaptus ruficollis* juveniles), featuring a relatively short neck and a proportionally large head relative to body size. Overall silhouette is slender with a distinctively rounded head profile.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform dark brownish-black body plumage with fine, dense vellus feathers. Juveniles are pale brownish-gray with less defined contrasts, featuring a duller overall appearance and less pronounced ear patches. Feather texture is smooth and slightly stiff, lacking the softness of many waterbird species; the plumage shows minimal sheen under natural light.  
Beak: Dark brown to black in color, moderately long for its body size, slender, and slightly curved distally with a sharp, pointed tip. The beak is robust enough for manipulating aquatic prey but lacks the pronounced hook seen in some other grebes.  
Eyes: Iris color is uniformly dark brown.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white with distinct, contrasting blackish "ear" patches (a key diagnostic feature) extending laterally from the eye. Base of the beak is dark brown, and no additional facial patches are present beyond the ear markings.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with a subtle, uniform sheen; texture is smooth and non-glossy. The abdominal region is relatively flat and lacks prominent barring or spotting.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a moderate span (approximately 40–45 cm). Primary feathers are dark brown, while secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown. Wing coverts are densely packed with fine, dark brown feathers.  
Tail: Short, rounded in shape, with a length of approximately 10–12 cm. Upper tail coverts are dark brown, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white. The tail lacks distinct streaming or elongation.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with moderately long, webbed feet (characteristic of grebes) and sharp, pointed claws. Feet are adapted for aquatic locomotion, with a moderate degree of webbing between the toes.

Body Size: Medium-sized grebe (45–50 cm total length), slightly smaller than *Tachybaptus fuscicollis* (Great Grebe) but larger than *Tachybaptus ruficollis* (Little Grebe). Streamlined, elongated body with a relatively short neck and robust torso, typical of diving grebes; overall outline is compact and dense for efficient underwater propulsion.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform dark brown upperparts with subtle iridescence; feather texture is smooth and slightly stiff. Juveniles are uniformly pale brown with less defined plumage, lacking the distinct pale throat patch and dark eye-rings of adults. Adults show a prominent pale yellowish throat patch bordered by dark brown, absent in juveniles.  
Beak: Dark gray to black, moderately long (approx. 50% of head length), slender with a slight decurved tip; base is robust and slightly swollen, transitioning to a fine, sharp apex. No visible "horn" (a common misconception; the head structure is a modified feather, not a true horn).  
Eyes: Iris color is dark brown.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellowish with a distinct dark brown eye-ring; base of the beak is dark brown, forming a smooth transition to the pale face. No specialized patches beyond the eye-ring.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with fine, short downy texture; lacks glossiness.  
Wings: Moderately long (approx. 150 mm), narrow and pointed with dark brown primaries and white secondary feathers; wing shape is adapted for rapid underwater maneuvering.  
Tail: Short (approx. 30 mm), rounded and slightly flattened; upper tail coverts are dark brown, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown, moderately slender; feet are fully webbed with strong, curved claws (no bare skin).

Body Size: Approximately 25–28 cm in total length (excluding tail), with a compact, streamlined body outline. The neck is relatively short and stiff compared to conspecifics like the Great Grebe (*Podiceps major*), resulting in a distinctive "short-necked" appearance. Overall, the bird exhibits a small, dense build with a proportionally large head relative to body size, typical of grebes adapted for aquatic foraging.

Body Plumage: Adults display a striking bipartite plumage pattern: a dark brown to blackish head and upper body with irregular white patches on the mantle and flanks, contrasting sharply with a pale buff to white underbody. Feather texture is dense, slightly stiff, and smooth, with fine vellus hairs on the body. Juveniles are uniformly dull brownish-gray with sparse, irregular white spotting on the mantle and flanks, lacking the defined black-and-white contrast of adults; plumage becomes more refined and contrasting with age, transitioning to the adult pattern by 12–15 months.

Beak: Black in color, with a distinct white tip (approximately 15–20% of beak length). The beak is stout, slightly curved at the base, and measures 30–35% of total body length. The tip is stiff and slightly hooked, facilitating precise manipulation of prey in shallow water. This beak morphology is a defining characteristic of the species and the source of its common name.

Eyes: Iris color is dark brown, lacking the bright hues seen in other aquatic birds (e.g., green in some ducks). The eyes are relatively small and positioned laterally on the head.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale buff to whitish, forming a distinct "mask" that contrasts with the dark beak base. The base of the beak is black, creating a sharp transition to the white tip. No specialized facial patches beyond the periorbital mask are present.

Abdomen: White to pale buff in color, with a subtle yellowish sheen in adults. Texture is smooth and non-glossy, with fine feathering along the edges. Juveniles exhibit a duller, more uniform brownish hue without the distinct white coloration.

Wings: Short, rounded wings (elliptical in shape) with a length of approximately 12–14 cm. Wing coloration is dark brown on the upper surfaces, with white flight feathers (remiges) visible in profile. The wings are relatively short and stiff, adapted for quick, agile movements in shallow water.

Tail: Short, measuring 5–6 cm in length. Shape is rounded and slightly flattened. Upper tail coverts are black, while under tail coverts are white, creating a contrasting visual effect. The tail is relatively short and stiff, with minimal feathering on the base.

Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with webbed feet (a characteristic feature of grebes) and sharp, pointed claws. The feet are moderately sized for the body, adapted for propulsion in water, with the webbing providing stability during diving and foraging. No specialized coloration or structural modifications beyond standard grebe morphology.

Body Size: Western Grebe (Tachybaptus polyphemus) measures 45–50 cm in total length, with a wingspan of 75–85 cm. It is slightly smaller and more robust than the closely related Eastern Grebe (Tachybaptus euryphorus), which averages 48–55 cm. The body outline is streamlined and elongated, optimized for efficient diving, with a relatively short neck and a deep, rounded chest cavity.  

Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a dark slate-blue to near-black upper body with a subtle iridescent sheen under direct light. The plumage is dense, smooth, and slightly glossy, with fine, interlocking barbs. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with duller, less saturated colors and lack the distinct adult plumage patterns; they gradually develop the adult's dark upperparts and white throat patch over 1–2 years.  

Beak: The beak is long (approximately 50–60% of body length), slender, and slightly curved distally. It is black in color with a fine, sharp tip and a moderately stout base. The beak lacks a pronounced hook, distinguishing it from other grebe species.  

Eyes: The iris is uniformly dark brown, with no visible color variation.  

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale grayish-white, forming a distinct pale stripe that extends from the base of the beak to the side of the head. The base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no white or red markings) present.  

Abdomen: The abdomen is pale yellowish-white with a soft, fluffy texture. It transitions gradually to a lighter buff color toward the vent, with no distinct barring or spotting.  

Wings: The wings are long (approximately 75–85 cm), narrow, and deeply curved, with a pointed tip. They are dark brown to black in color, featuring subtle pale feather edges that become more pronounced in flight. The wing structure is adapted for gliding but not for swimming.  

Tail: The tail is short (10–12 cm in length), rounded, and dark brown in color. The upper tail coverts are uniformly dark brown, while the under tail coverts are pale white with a slight yellowish tinge. The tail lacks a distinct central band or tuft.  

Legs and Feet: The legs are dark brown and moderately slender. The feet are fully webbed (palmate structure) with sharp, pointed claws, typical of diving birds. The webbing is dense and functional for propulsion in water.

Body Size: The Blue Grosbeak (*Pheucticus caeruleus*) measures 22–24 cm in length, exhibiting a robust, compact body outline that is slightly larger and more densely muscled than the closely related Indigo Bunting (*Passerina cyanea*). Its overall form is distinctly stocky with a relatively short neck and a heavy head, contributing to a compact, rounded silhouette when viewed from above.

Body Plumage: Adults display a vivid, iridescent cobalt blue body plumage (primarily on the upperparts and mantle) that transitions to a deep, rich blue on the ventral surface. The feathers possess a fine, slightly glossy texture with subtle structural coloration (iridescence) that enhances the blue hue under varying light angles. Juveniles are distinctly different, exhibiting a pale brownish-gray mantle with fine, dark brown streaking on the flanks and underparts, and a duller, less saturated blue on the head and upper body compared to adults.

Beak: The beak is robust, dark gray to black in color, with a moderately long, slightly curved tip that is distinctly hooked (recurved) at the distal end. It is relatively stout and conical, adapted for seed-crushing, with a slight constriction near the base.

Eyes: The iris is uniformly dark brown in color, lacking any distinct rings or patterns.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale flesh-colored, contrasting sharply with the dark blue plumage. The base of the beak is pale flesh-colored, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no white or black markings) distinguishing this species from others.

Abdomen: The abdomen is pale yellowish-white with fine, inconspicuous barring (subtle, short dark streaks) along the ventral surface, particularly noticeable in the central region. The texture is smooth and non-ribbed.

Wings: The wings are moderately long (spanning approximately 18–20 cm) and exhibit a pointed, slightly tapered shape. The primary feathers are dark blue with black tips, while the secondary feathers are a deep, rich blue with a narrow black band at the base. The coverts are uniformly dark blue.

Tail: The tail is short (approximately 6–7 cm in length) and graduated, with a distinct, narrow base. The upper tail coverts are a deep, rich blue with black tips, while the under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white with fine, dark barring.

Legs and Feet: The legs are slender and dark brown in color, with non-webbed feet typical of terrestrial birds. The toes are short and robust, ending in sharp, pointed claws (no webbing between toes).

Body Size: Medium-sized for a grosbeak, measuring 25–28 cm in length (males) and 27–30 cm (females); robust and conical in outline with a distinct tapering tail, slightly smaller than the Northern Grosbeak (*Laridus* spp.) but larger than the Blue Grosbeak (*Piranga* spp.).  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a striking black-and-white pattern: males have a glossy black head, neck, and upper body with a prominent white throat patch and a bright yellow patch on the throat; females are brownish-gray with pale underparts and subtle barring. Juveniles are duller, with pale brownish-gray upperparts, pale buff underparts, and no distinct yellow patch, transitioning to adult plumage over 1–2 years. Feathers are stiff with fine vellus hairs on the underparts.  
Beak: Dark brown to black, stout and slightly curved, measuring 15–18 mm in length; tip is blunt and slightly chisel-like, adapted for seed-cracking.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris.  
Face: Pale superciliary arch (above the eye), base of the beak is dark brown, and males display a distinct yellow throat patch (absent in juveniles and females).  
Abdomen: Pale buff with fine, irregular barring; texture is soft and slightly fluffy.  
Wings: Moderately long (12–15 cm span), rounded and slightly stiff; primary feathers are dark brown, with secondary feathers showing a pale buff base and dark tips; coverts are dark brown with pale edges.  
Tail: Long (10–12 cm), graduated with a distinct black upper tail coverts and white under tail coverts; tip is rounded.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown, strong and robust with sharp, non-webbed claws; adapted for terrestrial foraging.

Body Size: Medium-large for a finch, measuring 22–25 cm in total length with a robust, barrel-shaped body. Significantly heavier than congeneric species (e.g., Black-capped Vireo), exhibiting a dense, compact musculature that supports strong flight mechanics. Overall outline is distinctly rounded and somewhat bulky compared to slender finch relatives, with a relatively short neck and broad chest.

Body Plumage: Adults display a rich, slate-blue upperparts (including head, back, and rump) with a distinct contrast to the pale, ash-gray underparts. Feather texture is coarse and stiff, with a slightly glossy sheen on the upperparts. Juveniles are uniformly duller, featuring pale brownish-gray upperparts and pale buff underparts with subtle, irregular streaking; they lack the vivid blue of adults and have shorter, less defined plumage patterns. The contrast between the blue upperparts and gray underparts is a key diagnostic feature.

Beak: Stout, conical, and robustly built, measuring approximately 25–30 mm in length. Color is dark brown with a slight blackish hue at the base, tapering to a sharp, slightly curved tip that is fine but not pointed. The beak is proportionally large for the body size, reflecting the bird's seed-eating adaptations.

Eyes: Iris color is a deep, uniform brown with no visible rings or variations.

Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white, creating a distinct contrast against the dark brown beak base. No specialized facial patches or markings are present; the face is relatively clean and unadorned.

Abdomen: Pale grayish-brown in color, with a soft, slightly fluffy texture. The plumage is fine and uniform without prominent barring or streaking.

Wings: Moderately long (spanning approximately 30–35 cm), with a broad, rounded shape typical of grosbeaks. Flight feathers are dark brown with subtle, narrow blue edges on the primary feathers, creating a noticeable iridescent sheen in sunlight. The secondary feathers are uniformly dark brown.

Tail: Long and graduated, measuring approximately 15–18 cm in length. Upper tail coverts are dark brown with a faint, narrow blue band at the base. Under tail coverts are white with a pale brownish tinge, forming a distinct contrast against the dark tail feathers.

Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with strong, robust structure supporting the bird's terrestrial foraging habits. Feet are non-webbed, featuring sharp, pointed claws that are well-adapted for gripping bark and twigs. The tarsus (leg) is relatively short and sturdy.

Body Size: Medium-sized songbird (20–22 cm in length), slightly heavier than the Northern Cardinal (*Cardinalis cardinalis*) and more robustly built with a moderately rounded head and compact body outline. Overall silhouette is distinctly angular with a short, stiff neck and a relatively large head for its size.  
Body Plumage: Adult males exhibit a striking contrast: a vibrant, densely packed **crimson-red** breast patch (extending to the lower abdomen) against a predominantly **olive-green** upper body and **pale yellow** underparts. Feather texture is smooth with subtle iridescence; juveniles are uniformly **dull brownish-olive** with sparse, pale underparts and no red plumage, lacking the vivid contrast of adults.  
Beak: **Dark brownish-black** in color, conical and stout (length 15–18 mm), with a slightly **hooked tip** and a narrow, robust base. The beak is proportionally large relative to head size.  
Eyes: **Bright yellow** iris, unadorned by any distinct markings.  
Face: Periorbital area is **pale buff** with a clean, unbroken transition to the dark beak base. A distinct **blackish-brown patch** (approximately 2 mm in diameter) is present directly behind the eye, extending slightly toward the nape.  
Abdomen: **Pale yellowish-olive** in color, with fine, soft feather texture and minimal down. The lower abdomen transitions smoothly to the pale yellow underparts without significant contrast.  
Wings: Moderately long (span 25–28 cm), with a **broad, rounded shape** and a distinct **short, stiff primary flight feather** at the tip. Upperwing coverts are **dark brown**, while secondary coverts show a **subtle greenish sheen** under direct light.  
Tail: **Medium length** (12–14 cm), with a **short, rounded tip**. Upper tail coverts are **dark brown** with a slight olive undertone, and under tail coverts are **pale yellow** with fine, soft texture. Tail feathers are stiff and non-plumose.  
Legs and Feet: **Dark brown** in color, with **strong, sharp claws** and **non-webbed feet** adapted for perching and terrestrial movement. Feet are relatively short and robust for a songbird.

Body Size: Medium-sized alcid seabird with an elongated, streamlined compact body outline; overall slender yet robust torso, moderately larger than small auklet species, featuring a short neck and rounded breast, adapted for both coastal flight and underwater foraging. 
Body Plumage: Breeding adult presents uniform deep velvet black across head, neck and upperparts with dense, sleek, water-repellent feather texture; conspicuous large solid white wing patch on upperwing. Non-breeding adult shows mottled dusky grey and white on head and underparts. Juvenile plumage is dull sooty brownish-black with faint scaled feather edging, lacking the crisp white wing patch of mature individuals. 
Beak: Moderately short, slender and sharply pointed; culmen straight with a fine acute tip; breeding individuals have vivid coral-red bill with dark black cutting edges; non-breeding and juvenile beaks are dull dusky grey with faint reddish undertones. 
Eyes: Iris is deep dark brown, appearing nearly black under natural light. 
Face: Periorbital region covered with smooth black plumage without distinct eye rings; lores and bill base are unmarked, presenting a plain facial contour; no decorative plumes or contrasting facial patches. 
Abdomen: Breeding abdomen is pure deep black with tight, dense feather texture; non-breeding and juvenile individuals have pale greyish-white mottled abdominal plumage with soft downy underlayer for thermal insulation. 
Wings: Moderately long, pointed and narrow in shape, optimized for agile coastal flight and diving; upperwing predominantly black with a prominent rounded white speculum patch; underwing is uniformly dark greyish-black. 
Tail: Short, slightly rounded in shape; rectrices dark sooty black; upper tail coverts dense and glossy black, under tail coverts dark grey with fine soft feather texture, compact and neatly arranged. 
Legs and Feet: Legs are short, robust and bright crimson-red; fully webbed feet with strong, curved sharp claws, specialized for swimming, diving and gripping rocky cliff nesting ledges.

Body Size: Medium-large gull (45–50 cm in length), slightly larger than the Herring Gull (*Larus argentatus*) and more robust than the Ring-billed Gull (*Larus macroglossus*); overall outline is rounded with a relatively short, broad head and a moderately long, slightly tapered body tapering to a pointed tail.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a distinctive white body with a dark gray head and neck, featuring a prominent black "mask" (suborbital region) extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head; plumage texture is smooth and dense with fine, short feathers. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale streaking on the flanks and underparts, lacking the adult mask and displaying a more diffuse, less defined plumage pattern.  
Beak: Yellowish-orange in color, moderately long (approx. 50–60% of body length), slender with a slightly curved tip; the distal third is black, forming a distinct subterminal black spot on the upper mandible.  
Eyes: Dark brown irises.  
Face: Periorbital area is dark gray to black (the "mask"), contrasting sharply with the pale yellowish skin base of the beak; no specialized facial patches are present.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white in adults, smooth and relatively flat; juveniles show a more uniform brownish-yellow coloration with faint streaking.  
Wings: Long (approx. 120–140 cm), broad with a slightly rounded tip; primary feathers are dark gray to black with white tips, and secondary feathers are pale gray with distinct black subterminal spots.  
Tail: Short (approx. 15–20 cm), rounded and slightly upcurved; upper tail coverts are dark gray, while under tail coverts are white with a pale yellowish base.  
Legs and Feet: Yellowish-brown in color, moderately slender; feet are webbed (not clawed), with a short, robust tarsus and three functional toes.

Body Size: Adults measure 50–55 cm in length, with a wingspan of 110–120 cm. They exhibit a more streamlined, compact body outline compared to larger conspecifics like the Herring Gull (*Larus argentatus*), featuring a relatively short neck and a proportionally larger head relative to body mass. This morphology supports their agile foraging behavior in coastal and open marine environments.  

Body Plumage: Adults display a pale grayish-brown body plumage with fine, dense feathering that appears smooth and non-reflective under direct light. The plumage transitions from a duller gray on the ventral side to a darker, almost blackish-brown on the dorsal side. Juveniles are distinctly paler with a uniform brownish-gray hue, sparse streaking along the flanks, and less defined feather structure, gradually acquiring adult plumage over 2–3 years.  

Beak: Dark gray to black in color, with a moderately stout, slightly curved shape. The beak is relatively long for its body size (approximately 50% of total body length), featuring a sharp, pointed tip that is not excessively hooked. The base is robust and slightly swollen, consistent with their piscivorous diet.  

Eyes: Iris color is uniformly yellowish, lacking the reddish or brownish tones seen in many other gull species. This feature is particularly conspicuous against the pale facial plumage.  

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale grayish-white with a distinct, narrow pale patch extending posteriorly from the eye, creating a "smile-like" effect. The base of the beak is dark gray, contrasting sharply with the pale facial region. No specialized facial markings beyond this pale patch are present.  

Abdomen: White with faint, irregular brownish streaks along the ventral surface in adults; the texture is smooth and non-ribbed. Juveniles exhibit more pronounced, diffuse brownish streaking across the abdomen.  

Wings: Moderately long (110–120 cm wingspan), with a narrow, slightly curved shape. The leading edge (especially the upperwing coverts) displays a distinctive sky-blue (glaucous) coloration that is most intense in the central wing area, fading to pale gray on the trailing edges. The wingtips are white with a narrow blackish band.  

Tail: Short (approximately 15–18 cm in length), rounded and slightly upturned. Upper tail coverts are dark brown, while under tail coverts are white with a faint brownish tinge. The tail lacks prominent central feathers and shows minimal variation in color across the coverts.  

Legs and Feet: Dark gray in color, with webbed feet (typical of gulls) and three toes. The feet are moderately sized and adapted for wading in shallow water; no visible claws are present on the toes.

Body Size: Heermann's Gull (Larus heermannii) measures 45–50 cm in length, with a wingspan of 100–110 cm. It is notably smaller and more compact than the Herring Gull (Larus argentatus) of similar latitudes, exhibiting a relatively short, rounded head and a streamlined body outline typical of small gulls in the North Pacific.

Body Plumage: Adults display a distinct dark brownish-gray back and scapulars, contrasting with pale, sooty gray underparts that transition to a pale yellowish-white on the flanks and ventral side. Feather texture is smooth with fine, dense vane structure. Juveniles are uniformly pale gray-brown with a more pronounced dark brownish mantle and less defined pale underparts, lacking the adult's distinct coloration patterns.

Beak: Short, robust, and slightly decurved, with a dark gray base and a sharply black tip. The beak is moderately stout relative to head size and lacks a pronounced hook.

Eyes: Iris color is dark brown.

Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white with a distinct dark brownish eye stripe. The base of the beak is pale gray, and there are no prominent facial patches or markings.

Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with a subtle, uniform sheen; texture is smooth and non-iridescent.

Wings: Moderately short and rounded, with a dark brownish-gray coloration on the primary and secondary coverts, transitioning to pale grayish-white on the outer primaries and secondary feathers. The wingtips are pale.

Tail: Short, with a rounded tip. Upper tail coverts are dark brown, while under tail coverts are pale grayish-white. The tail lacks distinct barring or streaking.

Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with short, sturdy legs and non-webbed feet bearing sharp, pointed claws. Feet are adapted for perching and walking on rocky substrates.

Body Size: Medium-large gull (50–60 cm in length), with a robust, rounded body outline that tapers slightly toward the tail. Adults are consistently larger and more robust than juvenile conspecifics, with a relatively short neck and a body proportion that gives a distinctly "herring" silhouette compared to other gulls like the Great Black-backed Gull.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a pale grayish-brown back with subtle blackish streaking and a distinct white underparts with a pale yellowish wash on the flanks. Feather texture is smooth and slightly glossy, with fine vellus hairs on the underparts. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with dense, dark streaking on the back and pale, unmarked underparts, lacking the adult's distinct coloration and showing a more uniform, less defined plumage.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, stout and moderately long for body size, with a sharply curved, hooked tip that is slightly chisel-like. The beak base is robust and slightly swollen.  
Eyes: Yellowish iris with a pale central ring.  
Face: Pale, unmarked periorbital area (around the eyes), with a distinct dark eye stripe extending from the base of the beak to the side of the head. No specialized facial patches are present.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white in color, smooth and relatively flat texture, with minimal visible feathering.  
Wings: Long and broad, with a distinct "herring" wing profile; primary feathers are dark gray to black, while secondary feathers are pale gray with a subtle white margin. Wingtips are white, and the wings are relatively stiff and rigid.  
Tail: Short and rounded, with dark gray upper tail coverts and white under tail coverts that form a distinct "white tail patch" visible in flight. The tail is relatively short compared to other gull species.  
Legs and Feet: Dark gray in color, with webbed feet and sharp, pointed claws. The feet are moderately sized for the body and adapted for wading and swimming.

Body Size: Large for a gull, measuring 70–80 cm in length (excluding wingspan), with a robust, stocky build relative to its wingspan. Conspecifics (e.g., Herring Gulls) are smaller and more slender, while Ivory Gulls exhibit a distinctly compact, barrel-shaped outline with a short neck and broad chest, contributing to their dense, heavy-bodied appearance for Arctic foraging.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a uniform pale ivory-white body with subtle, fine-scale variation in hue (ranging from pale cream to near-off-white), featuring dense, soft, slightly curved feathers that lack the coarse texture of many other gulls. Face: The periorbital area is pale, almost whitish, with a distinct dark brownish patch at the base of the beak. No specialized facial markings beyond this; the face is relatively clean and unmarked.  

Abdomen: Pale white with faint, irregular brownish barring (subterminal) that becomes less pronounced toward the base. Texture is smooth and non-iridescent.  

Wings: Short, moderately pointed, with a distinct blue hue on the upper surface (slate-blue to deep blue) and pale brownish underparts. Wing length is approximately 12–14 cm, with a relatively short primary projection.  

Tail: Long (approximately 10–12 cm), graduated in shape, with black upper tail coverts bearing white tips (subterminal) and white under tail coverts. The tail is relatively stiff and rigid, typical of kingfishers.  

Legs and Feet: Dark brown to black in color, slender and relatively short. Feet are non-webbed, with three toes (hallux) and a single claw on each toe, adapted for perching on vertical surfaces.

Body Size: Approximately 18–20 cm in length (excluding tail), with a slender, streamlined body profile that is notably smaller and more delicate than the closely related Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis). The overall outline is elongated with a relatively short neck and a proportionally large head, giving it a distinctive "stubby" appearance compared to other kingfisher species.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a vibrant, uniform verdant green on the upperparts (crown, back, rachis), with a subtle iridescent blue sheen under direct light. The plumage is smooth, densely packed with fine, slightly curved barbs that produce a soft, velvety texture. Juveniles display a duller, brownish-grayish tone on the upperparts with pale, washed-out underparts and lack the intense green of adults; their plumage is also less glossy and more matte.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved (curved downward at the tip), with a robust base that transitions to a fine, sharp tip. The beak is predominantly black in color, with a distinct pale blueish-white tip that is slightly chisel-like for prey capture.  
Eyes: Iris is a vivid, clear blue with a narrow pale yellowish ring around the pupil.  
Face: The periorbital area (around the eye) is pale yellowish-white, contrasting sharply with the dark beak base. A distinctive, narrow white patch extends posteriorly from the eye, forming a "eyebrow" effect.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with a subtle, faint greenish sheen along the edges; texture is soft and slightly fluffy, lacking the dense downy covering seen in some other kingfisher species.  
Wings: Moderately short (approx. 12 cm in length), with a pointed, narrow shape and a slight curve at the tip. The primary feathers are dark green with a pale blueish edge, while the secondary feathers are uniformly greenish-blue. Wings are relatively stiff and show minimal movement during flight.  
Tail: Long (approx. 10 cm), graduated with a narrow base and a broad, flattened tip. Upper tail coverts are a deep, glossy green, while under tail coverts are pale white with a faint greenish tinge. The tail feathers are stiff and rigid, providing stability during rapid dives.  
Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown in color, with sharp, pointed claws (non-webbed). The feet are adapted for perching on small branches and aquatic substrates, with a relatively short tarsus and strong, curved claws for gripping.

Body Size: The Pied Kingfisher (*Ceryle rudis*) measures 25–28 cm in body length (excluding tail), exhibiting a slender, streamlined body typical of the kingfisher family (Alcedinidae). It is slightly smaller than the Common Kingfisher (*Alcedo atthis*) but proportionally more robust with a distinctively elongated neck and relatively short tail compared to other kingfisher species. The overall outline is compact yet agile, optimized for rapid aerial maneuvers and aquatic foraging.  

Body Plumage: Adults display a striking black-and-white plumage pattern with a predominantly white underbody and black head, neck, and upperparts. The plumage consists of stiff, glossy feathers with fine, uniform vellus texture; the white areas are immaculate and lack barring in mature birds. Juveniles exhibit a more subdued, brownish-tinged plumage with faint, irregular black markings on the head and neck, and the underparts are pale buff with subtle streaking, gradually transitioning to the adult pattern over 1–2 years.  

Beak: The beak is long (approximately 45–50% of body length), slender, and sharply pointed with a distinct, robust base. It is predominantly yellowish-gold in adults, fading to pale yellow at the tip, and features a slightly curved upper mandible with a fine, sharp apex ideal for capturing prey. The beak is relatively stiff and not webbed.  

Eyes: The iris is a deep, uniform brown, lacking any distinct color variation or reflective properties.  

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale grayish-white with a distinct, narrow white patch extending from the base of the beak to the side of the head. The base of the beak is dark brown, contrasting sharply with the pale periorbital region. No specialized facial markings (e.g., crests or tufts) are present.  

Abdomen: The abdomen is uniformly white with no barring or spotting in adults; juveniles show faint, irregular brownish streaks. The texture is smooth and non-iridescent, consistent with the overall plumage.  

Wings: The wings are short (approximately 12–14 cm in span) and rounded at the tips, with a dark brownish-black coloration on the upper surfaces and a pale white band along the trailing edges. The primary feathers are long and slightly curved, contributing to the bird’s agile flight.  

Tail: The tail is moderately long (approximately 10–12 cm) and graduated, with a distinct black upper tail coverts and white under tail coverts. The tail feathers are stiff and relatively short, providing stability during rapid dives.  

Legs and Feet: The legs are short and robust, with dark brown coloration. The feet are unwebbed, terminating in three functional claws (two on the inner toe, one on the outer toe), typical of kingfishers. No specialized adaptations for aquatic locomotion are present.

Body Size: The Ringed Kingfisher (*Alcedo cirrhos*) measures 18–20 cm in total length, exhibiting a compact, streamlined body outline that is notably smaller than the closely related Common Kingfisher (*Alcedo atthis*) but proportionally more robust than juvenile forms. Its body is slightly tapered distally with a relatively short neck, contributing to a distinctive "stubby" silhouette when viewed from above.

Body Plumage: Adults display a striking blue body plumage (specifically, a deep cerulean blue on the upperparts) with a narrow, pale white ring encircling the neck base. Feathers are smooth, glossy, and densely packed, with a subtle iridescence under direct light. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with faint, indistinct pale rings along the neck and chest, lacking the vivid blue of adults; their plumage is less glossy and more matte, with a duller overall sheen.

Beak: The beak is short, stout, and robustly curved, with a sharp, pointed tip ideal for capturing prey. It is predominantly dark grayish-blue in color, measuring approximately 15–18 mm in length, and exhibits a slight constriction at the base.

Eyes: The iris is a vivid, uniform yellow, contrasting sharply with the blue plumage and providing clear visual differentiation from other kingfisher species.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale yellowish-white, fading to a lighter hue at the base of the beak. The beak base is dark grayish-blue, and there are no distinct facial patches or markings beyond the pale periorbital region.

Abdomen: The abdomen is predominantly white with a subtle yellowish tinge, featuring a soft, fine texture and minimal feathering. It lacks distinct barring or spotting.

Wings: Wings are short and rounded, with a length of approximately 120–130 mm. The primary feathers are dark blue, while the secondary feathers are pale blue with white tips. The wingtips are distinctly white, and the overall wing profile is relatively narrow.

Tail: The tail is short (approximately 60–70 mm in length) and stiff, with dark grayish-blue upper tail coverts and white under tail coverts. The tail exhibits minimal feathering and a rigid, slightly flattened structure.

Legs and Feet: Legs are short and slender, with dark grayish-blue coloration. Feet are unwebbed, terminating in sharp, strong claws suitable for perching on rocky substrates, not aquatic environments.

Body Size: Approximately 20–25 cm in total length for adults, with a compact, streamlined body outline. Adults are consistently 10–15% larger in body mass than juveniles, exhibiting a proportionally shorter neck and more robust thorax compared to the closely related Blue Kingfisher (*Alcedo atthis*). The overall silhouette is characterized by a distinct head-to-body ratio with minimal abdominal fluff.  

Body Plumage: Adults display a striking contrast between a deep cerulean-blue back and scapulars, transitioning to a pale, unmarked white throat and breast. The plumage is densely packed with fine, interlocking barbs that produce a smooth, slightly glossy sheen under direct sunlight. Juveniles exhibit a duller, more variable plumage with brownish-grayish upperparts, pale buff underparts, and a faint streaking along the flanks, lacking the vivid cerulean of adults.  

Beak: Dark slate-blue to black in color, with a sharply curved, slightly hooked tip that is robust and adapted for fish capture. The beak length measures approximately 50–60% of total body length, with a narrow, sturdy base and a subterminal (slightly tapered) tip that facilitates precise prey manipulation.  

Eyes: Iris color is uniformly dark brown with a subtle golden sheen in optimal lighting conditions.  

Face: The periorbital area is pale grayish-white, sharply defined by the dark beak base. There are no distinct facial patches or markings; the transition from the pale face to the dark beak base is abrupt and clean.  

Abdomen: White with a faint, uniform yellowish tinge (especially in sunlit conditions), featuring a smooth, non-ribbed texture. The abdominal plumage is densely packed with short, fine feathers that lack the pronounced barring seen in other kingfisher species.  

Wings: Moderately short (approximately 10–12 cm in length), with a rounded, slightly tapered shape. The upperwing coverts are a vibrant cerulean-blue, while the flight feathers (remiges) are pale blue-gray with a subtle blackish tip. The wingtips are white, creating a distinct contrast against the darker body.  

Tail: Relatively long (approximately 12–15 cm), with a graduated, stiff structure. The upper tail coverts are a deep, uniform cerulean-blue, while the under tail coverts are pure white. The tail exhibits minimal feathering at the base, with a straight, slightly curved tip that aids in stability during flight.  

Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown in color, with sharp, non-webbed claws. The feet are adapted for perching rather than aquatic locomotion, featuring three toes (with the fourth toe reduced) and a robust, slightly curved claw tip for gripping substrates.

Body Size: Medium-sized gull (35–40 cm in length), slightly smaller than the common kittiwake (*Rissa tridactyla*); streamlined, elongated body with a relatively short neck and narrow thorax, giving a compact yet agile silhouette for aerial maneuvering.
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a predominantly white body with dark grayish-brown upperparts and blackish wings; feather texture is smooth with fine vane structure. Juveniles are uniformly pale brownish-gray with faint streaking on the flanks and a duller, less defined white underparts compared to adults; plumage becomes progressively whiter and more defined with each subsequent molt.
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, moderately long, slender, and slightly hooked at the tip; base is robust but not stout.
Eyes: Dark brown irises.
Face: Pale skin surrounding the eyes (periorbital area), with a distinct dark brownish-black base of the beak; no specialized facial patches or markings.
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white in color, smooth texture with fine, short downy feathers; minimal visible barring.
Wings: Long and narrow, with a pointed tip; upperwing coverts are dark gray to black, while the trailing edge is pale grayish-white.
Tail: Short, rounded in shape; upper tail coverts are dark gray to black, while under tail coverts are pale grayish-white with subtle barring.
Legs and Feet: Bright red in color (distinctive feature), slender and relatively short; feet are unwebbed with three toes (hallux) and two functional toes (second and third), ending in sharp, black claws.

Body Size: The Horned Lark (*Alaudala cetti*) exhibits a compact, robust body plan measuring 15–18 cm in length (excluding tail) and 25–30 g in mass. It is slightly smaller and more densely built than the closely related Rock Lark (*Alaudala canaries*), with a proportionally short neck and a body outline that is distinctly angular and less streamlined than many passerines. The overall silhouette is characterized by a short, stubby tail and a relatively large head relative to body size.

Body Plumage: Adults display a finely patterned rufous-brown upper body with a distinct pale superciliary stripe and a subtle, narrow rufous patch on the nape. The plumage is dense and fine-grained, with coarse guard hairs interspersed among the shorter body feathers. Juveniles are uniformly olive-brown with duller, less defined rufous accents, lacking the distinct nape patch and pale superciliary stripe of adults; their plumage is generally less structured and more uniformly muted.

Beak: The beak is short, robust, and slightly chisel-like in profile, measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length. It is dark grayish-brown in color, with a moderately stout base and a sharp, slightly hooked tip that is not webbed or flattened.

Eyes: The iris is uniformly dark brown, with no visible color variation or distinct markings.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) features a pale, narrow superciliary stripe (a distinct pale stripe above the eye) and a dark brown orbital ring. The base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no prominent facial patches or markings beyond the superciliary stripe.

Abdomen: The abdomen is pale buff to pale yellowish-brown in color, densely covered with fine, short feathers that exhibit subtle, irregular speckling of darker brown. The texture is soft and slightly velvety.

Wings: The wings are short and rounded, with a length of approximately 12–14 cm. The primary feathers are dark brown, and the secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown. The wing coverts are uniformly rufous-brown with fine, dark barring.

Tail: The tail is moderately long (approximately 10–12 cm) and graduated, with a distinct dark brown upper tail coverts (the outermost tail feathers) that have pale white tips. The under tail coverts are pale buff with fine, dark brown barring.

Legs and Feet: The legs are short, strong, and dark brown in color. The feet are unwebbed, with sharp, pointed claws that are adapted for terrestrial movement and digging. The tarsus (leg segment) is short and robust.

Body Size: Medium-small loon species, compact streamlined fusiform body outline; noticeably smaller than Common Loon and Yellow-billed Loon, with a slender neck, rounded chest, and tapered hindbody, exhibiting an elegant aquatic contour adapted for diving and migratory flight. 
Body Plumage: Breeding adult has smooth, glossy blackish-purple head and hindneck with fine greenish iridescence; upperparts dark greyish-black with neatly scaled pale grey feather fringes. Non-breeding adult loses iridescence, displaying dull grey upperparts and pale whitish foreneck. Juvenile plumage is muted dusky brownish-grey above with distinct pale scalloped edging, underparts cleaner white, lacking the adult’s iridescent sheen. 
Beak: Slender, moderately short, dagger-shaped with straight culmen and pointed tip; relatively fine and less stout than larger loon species; breeding and non-breeding adults have dark grey to black bill; juvenile bill is paler grey with a slight bluish hue at the base. 
Eyes: Iris is deep crimson red, vivid and conspicuous against dark facial plumage. 
Face: Periorbital region enveloped in dark iridescent head feathers without a distinct eye ring; lores and bill base unmarked; breeding plumage features a crisp pale grey demarcation line separating dark crown from pale throat, lacking bold spotting or facial patches. 
Abdomen: Abdominal region immaculate clean white with dense, soft, water-resistant downy feather texture; uniformly unstreaked, extending from lower breast to undertail, maintaining plain pale appearance in all age classes. 
Wings: Moderately long, narrow and pointed, built for swift direct flight; upperwing plain dark greyish-black with subtle muted feather margins; underwing pale silvery-grey along coverts, flight feathers dark grey, lacking conspicuous wing bars. 
Tail: Very short, bluntly rounded and wedge-shaped; rectrices dark sooty grey-black; upper tail coverts dark grey with fine pale edging, under tail coverts blend into white abdominal plumage, compact and tightly feathered. 
Legs and Feet: Legs short, compressed laterally, dark grey to bluish-grey in color; fully webbed palmate feet with strong, pointed curved claws; positioned far posterior on the body, specialized for underwater propulsion and limited awkward terrestrial locomotion.

Body Size: Medium-sized dabbling duck with a streamlined, elongated body profile; adults measure 48–55 cm in length (excluding bill) and weigh 450–700 g. Slightly smaller and more compact than larger dabbling ducks like the Pintail (Anas acuta), with a proportionally shorter neck and broader chest than the Mallard's conspecifics (e.g., the Northern Shoveler).

Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a striking sexual dimorphism: males display a rich, iridescent green head (with a prominent bronze sheen), a white chest with a dark brown "moustache" band, and a dark brown body with a pale yellowish belly. Females are mottled brown with a pale buff underbelly and a distinct dark brown "neck patch." Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale buff underparts, less pronounced sexual dimorphism, and a duller, less saturated plumage than adults; their head lacks the male's green sheen and body is more uniformly brown with faint streaking.

Beak: Stout, slightly decurved, and moderately long (approximately 35–40 mm); base is dark gray, tip is blunt and slightly hooked (not pointed), with a fine, keratinized texture.

Eyes: Iris color is dark brown in males and light brown in females.

Face: Periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale buff with a subtle, fine streaking; base of the beak is dark brown; no distinct facial patches or markings are present.

Abdomen: Pale yellowish to pale buff in color, smooth and relatively flat; texture is soft and slightly glossy, with minimal visible feathering.

Wings: Moderately long (approximately 25–30 cm), broad and rounded at the tips; primary feathers are dark brown with white tips, secondary feathers are pale brown with dark brown edges; overall wing coloration is dark brown with a pale buff underwing.

Tail: Moderately long (approximately 15–18 cm), short and rounded; upper tail coverts are blackish-brown with white tips in males, pale brown in females; under tail coverts are pale brown in females and dark brown with white tips in males.

Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color; feet are webbed (as typical for dabbling ducks), with strong, pointed claws; the webbing is moderately dense, facilitating propulsion in water.

Body Size: Western Meadowlark (*Sturnella neglecta*) exhibits a compact, slender body plan measuring 20–22 cm in total length (excluding tail) with a wingspan of 30–35 cm. Compared to conspecifics (e.g., Eastern Meadowlark), it is slightly smaller and more streamlined, with a relatively narrow thorax and a distinctive "conspicuous" silhouette when perched in open grasslands due to its contrasting plumage against the substrate.  

Body Plumage: Adults display a striking yellowish-white breast with fine black streaking, contrasting sharply with a brownish-gray back and rufous-brown flanks. Feather texture is smooth and slightly stiff on the body (vellus feathers), with a glossy sheen on the head and upperparts. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with faint, diffuse streaking on the breast and a duller yellowish wash on the flanks, lacking the distinct black streaking of adults; plumage matures to adult patterns within 2–3 breeding seasons.  

Beak: Dark grayish-brown in color, with a short, slightly downcurved tip and a moderately stout base. The beak length is approximately 12–14 mm, proportionally short for its body size, and features a subtle, fine hook at the tip adapted for seed processing.  

Eyes: Iris color is a pale yellowish-green in adults, with a slight metallic sheen under natural light.  

Face: Features a distinct pale yellowish supercilium (eyebrow stripe) extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head, a narrow dark eye-ring, and pale skin around the orbital region. The base of the beak is pale yellow, contrasting with the darker facial plumage.  

Abdomen: Solid yellowish-white with a subtle brownish tinge at the edges, smooth texture without prominent barring. The coloration is uniform and non-glossy.  

Wings: Moderately long (approx. 150 mm), with pointed tips and a slight curvature. Upperwing coverts are dark brown, while the flight feathers (remiges) are pale brown with blackish tips. The wing profile is relatively narrow, typical of open-country foragers.  

Tail: Moderately long (approx. 100 mm), graduated in shape with a slightly convex tip. Upper tail coverts are dark brown with white tips, while under tail coverts are pale yellow with fine brownish edges. The tail exhibits a distinct "notched" appearance when viewed from above.  

Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender with non-webbed feet. Tarsus length is approximately 25 mm, and the feet end in sharp, pointed claws (no webbing), consistent with terrestrial foraging behavior.  

*Note: All descriptions adhere strictly to the *Sturnella neglecta* (Western Meadowlark) species as documented in the *Checklist of North American Birds* (2023) and *The Birds of North America* (v. 2.0), with emphasis on visual field identification under natural conditions.*

Body Size: Medium-sized diving duck (45–50 cm total length), slightly smaller than the Common Merganser (*Mergus lyricus*) but larger than the Northern Shoveler (*Anas clypeata*). Streamlined, elongated body with a relatively short neck and compact thorax, presenting a robust, aquatic-adapted outline for efficient underwater foraging.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a distinctive black hood with a narrow white superciliary stripe, contrasting with a pale brownish-gray body and a white neck patch. Feathers are densely packed with fine, stiff vane structure, providing hydrodynamic efficiency. Juveniles are uniformly brown with mottled white spots on the flanks and a pale, unmarked neck, lacking the hooded pattern; plumage becomes glossy and darker with age.  
Beak: Dark brown to black in color, moderately long (3–4 cm), slightly decurved, with a sharp, pointed tip adapted for gripping prey. The beak is stout relative to head size but not webbed.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris.  
Face: Pale, unmarked periorbital area with a distinct dark eye stripe; base of the beak is dark brown, contrasting sharply with the pale face. No specialized facial patches.  
Abdomen: White with a subtle yellowish sheen in adults; smooth, non-iridescent texture.  
Wings: Long (approx. 35 cm), broad with a rounded tip, featuring dark brown primaries and white secondaries. The wing profile is streamlined for rapid underwater propulsion.  
Tail: Short (approx. 10 cm), rounded tip; upper tail coverts are dark brown, while under tail coverts are white with faint brownish edges.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown coloration; feet are webbed with strong, pointed claws (not flattened), adapted for gripping substrates during diving.

Body Size: Adult males measure 45–50 cm in total length with a streamlined, elongated body outline that is slightly shorter and more compact than the male Common Merganser (*Mergus serrator*), yet distinctly larger than the female Red-breasted Merganser. The body proportions are optimized for aquatic foraging, featuring a relatively narrow thorax and a deep, robust abdomen relative to wing span.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a dark slate-gray head and neck with a prominent pale buff stripe along the superciliary region, contrasting sharply with a vivid crimson patch on the upper breast (reaching the mid-axillary area) and a pale yellowish-white abdomen. Feathers are densely packed with fine, slightly curved barbs, giving a matte, non-glossy texture. Juveniles lack the crimson breast patch, displaying duller grayish-brown plumage with sparse, pale barring on the flanks and a pale buffish wash on the ventral side.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, moderately long (10–12 cm), slightly decurved with a sharp, pointed tip that is robust and adapted for gripping fish. The beak base is broad and slightly flattened, with a fine, keratinized edge.  
Eyes: Iris is a deep, uniform brown with no distinct color variation.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale buff with a distinct dark brown stripe extending from the eye to the base of the beak. The base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches or markings beyond the periorbital stripe.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with fine, inconspicuous dark brown barring (1–2 bars) along the ventral surface. Texture is smooth and non-glossy, with minimal downy covering.  
Wings: Moderately long (span of 60–70 cm), broad with a slightly rounded leading edge. Flight feathers (remiges) are dark brown to black, tipped with white, and the coverts are pale gray with subtle barring.  
Tail: Short (approximately 15 cm), rounded in shape. Upper tail coverts are dark brown with a pale buffish edge, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white with fine, dark barring.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with webbed feet (adapted for aquatic locomotion) and no visible claws. The tarsus is moderately robust, and the feet are covered in dense, short feathers.

Body Size: Medium-sized songbird (30–35 cm in length), slightly larger than female conspecifics with a robust, rounded body outline and a relatively short, heavy neck. Overall proportions exhibit a characteristic bulky torso with a long, graduated tail, contrasting with the more slender build of smaller *Passer* species.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a glossy black upper body with a distinct white underbody and pale throat; feather texture is dense and slightly stiff, lacking the softness of *Icterus* species. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale streaking on the flanks and a duller, less glossy sheen than adults.  
Beak: Black, stout, and slightly curved at the tip (18–22 mm in length), with a robust base and a sharp, non-webbed tip.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris in adults; juveniles exhibit a pale yellowish-brown iris.  
Face: Pale buff periorbital area with a distinct pale stripe extending from the base of the beak to the throat; base of the beak is dark, and no specialized facial patches (e.g., wattles or epaulets) are present.  
Abdomen: White with fine, pale brownish streaking in adults; texture is smooth and non-ribbed, lacking dense down. Juveniles show more pronounced, darker streaking.
