Legs and Feet: Dark brown coloration; slender and relatively short; feet are unwebbed with sharp, pointed claws adapted for terrestrial movement and digging.

Body Size: Small to medium passerine sparrow with a robust, stocky compact body outline; bulkier and longer-bodied than most grassland sparrows, featuring a rounded head, thick neck, deep chest, and sturdy torso morphologically adapted to coastal saltmarsh habitats. 
Body Plumage: Adult upperparts display muted grayish-olive and dusky brown base with fine blurred dark streaking; feather texture dense, coarse, and cryptically blended for marsh camouflage. Overall plumage lacks strong contrasting patterns. Juvenile plumage is warmer buff-brown overall with more prominent diffuse streaking across upperparts and underparts, paler and less gray-toned than definitive adult plumage. 
Beak: Moderately elongated, conical, relatively slender at the base with a straight culmen and pointed tip; slightly longer and less stout than typical field sparrows; upper mandible dusky grayish-brown, lower mandible pale bluish-gray with faint flesh tint at base. 
Eyes: Iris is deep dark brown, uniformly pigmented and unadorned. 
Face: Periorbital region lacks a distinct eye-ring, covered in plain grayish-olive feathering; lores and bill base are pale grayish-buff; auricular patch is subdued and unmarked, with a faint thin pale malar stripe and no bold facial patches or strong head striping. 
Abdomen: Median abdomen is pale grayish-white with dense soft downy feather texture; flanks and lower belly exhibit thick, blurred dusky brown streaks; ventral plumage shows muted tonal blending without sharp barring. 
Wings: Moderately short, rounded and broad in shape, adapted for low, short flight within dense marsh vegetation; wing coverts dusky olive-brown with indistinct buff fringes; flight feathers dark brown with subtle grayish-olive edging, lacking conspicuous wing bars. 
Tail: Medium-length, slightly rounded and graduated in shape; rectrices dark dusky brown with narrow pale buff margins; upper tail coverts grayish-olive with fine dark streaking; under tail coverts pale buff with diffuse brown mottling. 
Legs and Feet: Legs relatively long, sturdy, pale pinkish-brown to grayish-flesh color; anisodactyl non-webbed feet with slender, sharply curved claws, adapted for walking on marsh mud, perching on cordgrass stems, and navigating saturated coastal vegetation.

Body Size: Song Sparrows (Melospiza melodia) exhibit a compact body size, typically measuring 12–15 cm in length (excluding tail) and weighing 12–18 g. They are slightly smaller and more slender than the closely related House Sparrow (*Passer domesticus*), with a relatively short, rounded body outline and a proportionally large head relative to body mass.  

Body Plumage: Adults display a rufous-brown to chestnut-brown base plumage on the upperparts, densely streaked with darker brown and blackish-brown markings. The underparts are pale buff to whitish with fine, dense streaking that transitions to a pale buff wash on the flanks. Juveniles are uniformly pale buff with faint, diffuse streaking and lack the distinct dark streaking of adults; their plumage is less saturated and more uniformly pale, with a duller overall appearance.  

Beak: Short, conical, and slightly robust, with a fine, pointed tip. The beak is moderately stout for a passerine, measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length, and exhibits a subtle, fine hook at the distal end.  

Eyes: Iris color is uniformly dark brown, with no distinct variation between sexes or age classes.  

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale buff to whitish, with a distinct pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head. The base of the beak is pale, and males possess a conspicuous white throat patch (a single, unbroken patch) contrasting sharply with the dark brown head and neck.  

Abdomen: Pale buff to creamy-white in color, with a fine, short vellus texture and minimal visible down. The abdomen is relatively flat and lacks distinct color variation.  

Wings: Short and rounded, with a moderate length (approximately 60–70% of body length). The primary feathers are dark brown, and the secondary feathers are pale buff with a subtle dark brown band along the leading edge. The wing profile is characteristically narrow and slightly curved.  

Tail: Moderately long (approximately 12–15 mm), with a short, rounded tip. The upper tail coverts are dark brown to blackish-brown, while the under tail coverts are pale buff with a faint dark brown streak. The tail exhibits a distinct subterminal band of pale buff on the outermost feathers.  

Legs and Feet: Short, slender, and dark brown in color. The feet are unwebbed, with sharp, pointed claws that are moderately robust for their size. The tarsus (leg) is short and robust relative to the body.

Body Size: 12–14 cm in length, with a compact, rounded body outline that is slightly smaller and more robust than the House Sparrow (*Passer domesticus*) conspecific. The overall form is slender yet dense, with a relatively short neck and a proportionally large head for its size.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a finely textured, medium-coarse vellus plumage with a base color of grayish-brown on the upperparts and pale buff-white on the underparts. Juveniles display a more mottled appearance with brownish-gray upperparts, pale buffy underparts, and distinct streaking along the flanks, fading to a uniform grayish-brown as they mature. The plumage is consistently soft and dense, with minimal sheen.  
Beak: Short, conical, and robust with a dark grayish-black coloration; the tip is slightly hooked and blunt, measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length. The beak is stout relative to the head size and lacks a visible webbed base.  
Eyes: Iris color is uniformly brownish-gray with a subtle yellowish tint in the central region, fading to a pale gray at the periphery.  
Face: Features a distinct pale superciliary arch (eyebrow ridge) above the eye, a narrow dark eye stripe, and a pale cere (the fleshy area at the base of the beak) that is typically yellowish-white. The face is relatively narrow with minimal facial feathering.  
Abdomen: Pale buff-white with fine, inconspicuous brownish streaks along the ventral side; texture is soft and fluffy, with minimal visible down.  
Wings: Moderately short and rounded, with a length of approximately 60–70 mm; the primary feathers are dark brown, while the secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown. The wing coverts are densely feathered with a uniform brownish hue.  
Tail: Relatively long (approximately 70–80% of body length), with a graduated shape that tapers to a fine point. Upper tail coverts are dark brown, while the under tail coverts are pale white with a faint brownish tinge. The central tail feathers are white, contrasting sharply with the darker upper tail coverts.  
Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown in color, with bare skin extending to the base of the tarsus; feet are non-webbed, with three toes (two forward, one backward) and sharp, pointed claws adapted for terrestrial movement.

Body Size: Small passerine with a body length of 12–14 cm; slightly smaller than the House Sparrow (*Passer domesticus*) but comparable in outline to the Song Sparrow (*Melospiza melodia*), exhibiting a compact, rounded body with a relatively short neck and a proportionally large head.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a finely streaked brownish-gray upper body with pale buffish streaks on the flanks and undertail coverts; feather texture is soft and dense, with subtle barbules creating a slightly velvety appearance. Juveniles are paler overall, with more prominent buff streaking on the crown and scapulars, and less defined barring on the flanks compared to adults.  
Beak: Short, slender, and conical with a dark gray base; tip is slightly chisel-like and robust for seed processing, measuring approximately 8 mm in length.  
Eyes: Iris is a uniform dark brown with no distinct color variation.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-buff with fine, irregular streaking; base of the beak is dark gray, and there are no distinct facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with fine, inconspicuous brownish streaks along the ventral side; texture is soft and slightly glossy.  
Wings: Moderately short (approx. 60% of body length), rounded at the tips, with a dark brownish-gray coloration on the upper surfaces and pale buffish underwings; primary feathers are slightly longer than secondary feathers.  
Tail: Short (approx. 45% of body length), graduated with a slightly flattened tip; upper tail coverts are dark brown with pale buffish edges, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white with fine brownish streaking.  
Legs and Feet: Dark grayish-brown in color; legs are short and sturdy with non-webbed feet, featuring sharp, pointed claws suitable for terrestrial movement.

Body Size: Slightly smaller than the House Sparrow (*Passer domesticus*) with a body length of 12–14 cm (4.7–5.5 in) and a wingspan of 18–20 cm (7.1–7.9 in). Overall outline is compact and robust, with a relatively short neck and a distinctly rounded head profile compared to similar *Zonotrichia* species.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a pale grayish-brown body with fine vellus hair texture; the upperparts are slightly darker (grayish-brown) than the underparts. Juveniles are uniformly pale grayish-brown with minimal contrast, lacking the distinct crown patterns and showing less defined streaking. Adults display a striking black-and-white crown pattern (two black stripes with white centers) and a pale grayish-brown throat.  
Beak: Short, conical, and slightly robust (length ~10 mm), with a sharp, chisel-like tip adapted for seed processing. The base is pale grayish-brown.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris with a subtle yellowish sheen in some individuals.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-brown with a distinct, narrow white supercilium (eyebrow stripe) and a dark eye stripe. The base of the beak is pale grayish-brown, and no prominent facial patches exist beyond the supercilium.  
Abdomen: Pale grayish-brown with fine, irregular streaking that fades to a lighter tone toward the vent. Texture is soft and slightly fluffy.  
Wings: Moderately short (length ~70 mm), with a rounded wing tip. Primary feathers are dark grayish-brown, and secondary feathers show subtle white tips visible in flight.  
Tail: Moderately long (length ~50 mm), with a broad, rounded tip. Upper tail coverts are grayish-brown, while under tail coverts are pale grayish-white with fine streaking.  
Legs and Feet: Short, slender, and slightly robust (color: pale grayish-brown). Feet are unwebbed with sharp, pointed claws adapted for terrestrial movement.

Body Size: Adults measure 14–16 cm in length with a body mass of 12–15 g. They exhibit a compact, somewhat rounded body outline with a relatively short neck and a slightly tapered breast. Compared to conspecifics (e.g., House Sparrows *Passer domesticus*), White-throated Sparrows are notably smaller and less robust, with a more slender overall silhouette that facilitates agile foraging in dense vegetation.  

Body Plumage: Adults display a distinctive pale buff to pale grayish-brown upper body with fine, subtle streaking on the back and flanks. The throat is a prominent, unbroken white patch (the most diagnostic feature), contrasting sharply with the darker head and breast. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with dense, fine streaking on the underparts and a pale buff throat lacking the adult white patch. Feather texture is soft and slightly downy, with a subtle gloss in the light. The male exhibits a brighter, more vivid white throat compared to the duller female plumage.  

Beak: Short, conical, and slightly decurved at the tip. Color is dark grayish-brown, with a fine, sharp apex that is not chisel-like. Length is approximately 10–12 mm, and the beak is relatively stout for its size, adapted for seed and insect consumption.  

Eyes: Iris color is a uniform, pale brown (not yellow or dark), with a subtle reflective sheen in low light.  

Face: Periorbital area is pale buff with a distinct, narrow dark brown eye stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head. The base of the beak is pale, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no white or black markings) distinguishing it from other sparrows.  

Abdomen: Clean white in adults, with minimal streaking. Juveniles show fine, dark brown streaking across the abdomen. Texture is soft and smooth, with a slight downy feel.  

Wings: Moderately short and rounded, with a length of approximately 70–80 mm. The wing coverts are dark brown, and the primary feathers are pale buff with a subtle blackish tip. The overall wing pattern is relatively subdued, aiding in camouflage against forest floors.  

Tail: Moderately long (approximately 50–60 mm), with a graduated shape. Upper tail coverts are dark brown, while the outermost tail feathers are white. Under tail coverts are pale buff with a faint white edge. The tail exhibits a subtle, narrow white band at the base.  

Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with short, sturdy claws (not webbed). The feet are adapted for terrestrial movement, with a slight curvature at the toes for grasping twigs. No webbing is present.

Body Size: Compact passerine with a total length of 15–17 cm; slightly smaller than the African Starling (*Lerista*) but larger than juvenile specimens. Overall outline is rounded and robust with a short neck and relatively large head proportionate to body size.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a deep, iridescent black body with a metallic sheen (bronze to blue-black) under direct sunlight; feather texture is smooth and densely packed with fine vellus hairs. Juveniles display duller, brownish-gray plumage with pale streaks on the flanks and a less pronounced sheen, transitioning to adult plumage within 3–4 months.  
Beak: Short, stout, and slightly curved with a dark black coloration; length measures 10–12 mm, featuring a sharp, chisel-like tip adapted for insect manipulation.  
Eyes: Iris is uniformly dark brown with minimal variation.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white with a distinct pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head; base of the beak is dark brown, and no specialized facial patches are present.  
Abdomen: White with faint, irregular brownish streaks; texture is soft and slightly fluffy, especially in the central region.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a length of 8–10 cm; primary feathers are dark brown with pale tips, while secondary feathers are uniformly pale gray.  
Tail: Short (5–6 feathers), black in color with white tips on the outermost feathers; upper tail coverts are dark brown with subtle white edging, and under tail coverts are pale white with minimal barring.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color; feet are slender with sharp, non-webbed claws, typical of terrestrial passerines.

Body Size: Bank Swallows (Rupicola riparia) exhibit a compact, streamlined body plan measuring 12–14 cm in length (excluding tail) and 25–30 g in mass. They are slightly smaller than the Eastern Meadowlark but comparable in size to the Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor), with a proportionally short neck and a slender, aerodynamic silhouette optimized for agile aerial foraging.

Body Plumage: Adults display a pale grayish-brown upperparts with fine, dense vellus feathers and subtle blackish-brown streaking on the flanks. The underparts are pale buff with distinct, fine, dark brown streaking along the flanks and breast. Juveniles are duller, featuring a more uniform brownish-gray head and body with less defined streaking and a pale buffish wash on the ventral side, transitioning to adult plumage within 2–3 breeding seasons.

Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved, with a blackish tip. The beak is moderately stout for their size (approximately 12–15 mm in length) and exhibits a sharp, pointed tip adapted for probing soil and capturing insects.

Eyes: Dark brown irises, contrasting with the pale facial plumage.

Face: Features a pale, narrow superciliary arch (eyebrow ridge) above the eyes. The base of the beak is pale grayish-brown, and there are no distinct facial patches; the face is generally pale with minimal contrast to the head plumage.

Abdomen: Pale buff with fine, irregular dark brown streaking, particularly concentrated along the central and ventral regions. The texture is soft and slightly fluffy.

Wings: Moderately short (approximately 100–110 mm in length) with a rounded, slightly tapered tip. The primary feathers are pale grayish-brown, and the secondary feathers exhibit a subtle blueish tinge at the tips, with the coverts being pale grayish-brown.

Tail: Relatively long (approximately 100–110 mm) and graduated, with a distinct white outer tail feather (subterminal white). The upper tail coverts are pale grayish-brown with fine blackish-brown streaking, while the under tail coverts are pale buff with subtle dark brown streaking.

Legs and Feet: Short, slender legs with sharp, non-webbed feet. The toes are moderately long and adapted for perching, with strong, pointed claws (no webbing) that facilitate quick takeoffs and secure perching on vertical surfaces.

Body Size: Medium-sized swallow (10–11 cm in length), slightly smaller than the House Swallow (*Hirundo rustica*) but comparable in overall proportions to the European Swallow (*Hirundo rustica*). Streamlined, tapered body with a relatively short neck and slender torso, exhibiting a characteristic swallow-like silhouette with minimal bulk.

Body Plumage: Adult males display a striking **cerulean blue** upperparts with a glossy sheen under direct light; underparts are pale buff with fine, dark brownish streaking. Feathers are smooth, densely packed, and exhibit a subtle iridescence in the blue hue. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray above with pale, streaked underparts (dark brownish streaks on pale buff), lacking the vivid blue and showing a more muted, less glossy appearance. The plumage transitions from juvenile to adult via a distinct intermediate phase with faint blue tints on the wings.

Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved at the tip (not sharply hooked), measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length. Color is dark grayish-brown, with a fine, sharp tip that is slightly chisel-like for probing insects.

Eyes: Iris color is a bright, uniform **yellow**.

Face: Periorbital area is pale buff with a clean, unbroken transition to the head. Base of the beak is dark grayish-brown, and there are no distinct facial patches or markings; the face is relatively featureless compared to other swallow species.

Abdomen: Pale buff with fine, irregular brownish streaking (especially prominent in juveniles), texture is soft and slightly velvety.

Wings: Moderately long (spanning approximately 15–17 cm), with a pointed, slightly curved shape. Primary feathers are dark grayish-brown with a subtle blue sheen at the base; secondary feathers are pale blue with dark tips. Wing coverts are dark brown, and the entire wing profile is streamlined for agile flight.

Tail: Long (approximately 60–70% of body length), distinctly forked with a slight curve at the base. Upper tail coverts are a vivid cerulean blue, matching the back plumage. Under tail coverts are pale buff with fine, dark streaking. The tail exhibits a characteristic "forked" structure with 10–12 feathers on each side.

Legs and Feet: Short, slender, and dark grayish-brown in color. Feet are unwebbed with three toes (hallux) and a single claw (not webbed), adapted for perching on vertical surfaces and quick movement. The claws are sharp and slightly curved.

Body Size: Cliff Swallows (Petrochelidon pyrrhonota) exhibit a compact body size averaging 10–11 cm in length (excluding tail) and 18–20 g in mass. They are notably smaller than congeneric species like the House Swallow (Apus apus) but share a streamlined, aerodynamic silhouette with a relatively short neck and slender body proportions, optimized for agile aerial foraging.  

Body Plumage: Adults display a distinctive blackish-brown head and upper body with a pale, unbroken white underbody and rump, featuring a subtle sheen on the back. The plumage is smooth and densely packed with fine, slightly stiff vane feathers, exhibiting a pale grayish-brown hue on the mantle. Juveniles are uniformly duller, with pale grayish-brown upperparts, a faintly streaked white underbody, and less defined contrasts; they lack the sharp blackish-brown head of adults and show a more uniform pale buff coloration on the flanks.  

Beak: The beak is short, slender, and slightly decurved, measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length. It is dark brown to black in color, with a fine, pointed tip and minimal visible keratin flaking. The beak is relatively stout for its size, supporting efficient insect handling.  

Eyes: The iris is uniformly dark brown, lacking any distinct color variation or reflective properties.  

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale grayish-white with a distinct, narrow pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head. The base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches or markings; the face is generally clean and unmarked.  

Abdomen: The abdomen is pale yellowish-white with a soft, fine texture and minimal downy covering. In adults, it shows a subtle, uniform pale yellowish hue without distinct barring or streaking. Juveniles exhibit a paler, more buff-colored abdomen with slightly coarser texture.  

Wings: Wings are moderately long (approximately 120–130 mm) and sharply pointed, adapted for rapid, agile flight. The primary feathers are dark brown with pale tips, while the secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown with distinct blackish-brown tips. The wing coverts are uniformly pale grayish-brown.  

Tail: The tail is long (approximately 60–70 mm) and graduated, with a distinct blackish-brown upper tail coverts and a white under tail coverts. The tail feathers are relatively stiff and show minimal variation in color across the length, with the outermost pair being pale grayish-white.  

Legs and Feet: Legs are short and slender, with dark brown coloration. Feet are unwebbed, featuring three toes (two forward, one backward) and sharp, pointed claws. The feet are adapted for perching on vertical surfaces but lack webbing, consistent with their cliff-dwelling habitat.

Body Size: Medium-sized passerine with a body length of 16–18 cm; slender and elongated compared to other swallow species (e.g., House Swallow), exhibiting a relatively narrow thorax and a distinctly pointed head profile that contributes to an overall streamlined, aerodynamic silhouette.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a vibrant, uniform cobalt blue upper body with a smooth, glossy sheen; underparts are pale blue-white with a subtle buffish tinge on the flanks. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray above with pale buff underparts, lacking the intense blue of adults and featuring a less defined facial pattern; feather texture is fine and dense, with minimal downy covering on the body.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved (curved downward at the tip), with a dark grayish-black coloration; tip is sharp and slightly hooked, measuring approximately 12–14 mm in length.  
Eyes: Iris is a bright, unadulterated yellow.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale with a distinct dark eye stripe; base of the beak is pale yellowish, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no black markings or wattles).  
Abdomen: Pale blue-white with a faint, uniform buffish wash on the lower abdomen; texture is smooth and non-iridescent.  
Wings: Moderately long (span of 22–25 cm), with a pointed tip; primary feathers are dark blue-black, secondary feathers are pale blue, and the wing coverts are a uniform, pale blue-gray.  
Tail: Short (approximately 50–60% of body length), narrowly graduated; upper tail coverts are a vivid cobalt blue, while under tail coverts are pure white with no barring or streaking.  
Legs and Feet: Short, slender, with bare skin on the lower legs (pale yellowish); feet are unwebbed, with three toes (two forward, one backward) and sharp, pointed claws.

Body Size: Medium-sized songbird (18–20 cm in length), with a slender, elongated body outline. Slightly more compact than the male Scarlet Tanager *Piranga olivacea* (which averages 19–21 cm) but distinctly less robust than the female *Piranga olivacea* (20–22 cm). Overall silhouette is triangular with a pointed head and relatively short neck.  
Body Plumage: Males exhibit a vibrant, uniform crimson-red plumage (PMS: 100–110) across the entire body, with no barring, streaking, or variation. Juveniles are olive-green above with pale yellowish underparts and faint brownish streaking on the flanks. Feather texture is smooth with fine vellus hairs on the body, and the plumage is densely packed without significant downy cover.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved (tip moderately hooked), measuring 10–12 mm in length. Color is uniformly black throughout, with no pale or pigmented base.  
Eyes: Iris is a bright, unadulterated yellow (PMS: 100–110), contrasting sharply with the red plumage.  
Face: Periorbital area is clean and unmarked, with no distinct facial markings. Base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized patches (e.g., no white or blue patches) on the head or neck.  
Abdomen: Solid crimson-red in males, smooth and uniform without any white, buff, or pale transitions. Texture is consistent with the rest of the body plumage (dense, smooth vellus).  
Wings: Moderately long (span 25–28 cm), with pointed tips and a slight curvature. Primary feathers are dark brown-black, while secondary feathers and coverts display vivid crimson-red. Wing coverts are densely packed with red plumage, showing minimal variation in hue.  
Tail: Moderately long (10–12 cm), with a broad, graduated shape tapering distally. Upper tail coverts are uniformly crimson-red, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white. Tail feathers are stiff and relatively rigid, with no significant fluffy or soft plumage.  
Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown in color, with sharp, pointed claws (no webbing). Feet are adapted for perching and terrestrial movement, typical of terrestrial songbirds.

Body Size: 15–17 cm in length, slightly smaller than the closely related Scarlet Tanager (*Pachycephala*); compact, streamlined body with a relatively short neck and a proportionally large head, giving a robust yet agile silhouette for its size.  
Body Plumage: Adult males exhibit a vibrant, metallic yellow plumage (with a subtle iridescent sheen under direct light) across the body, featuring dense, fine barbules that create a smooth, glossy texture; juveniles are duller, with brownish-yellow head and body, transitioning to bright yellow by the second year.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly curved at the tip (approximately 10 mm in length), with a fine, sharp tip and a moderately stout base; no visible webbing.  
Eyes: Iris is a vivid, uniform red (not reddish-brown) with a dark brown sclera.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellow with a distinct, narrow pale stripe above the eye (superciliary region); base of the beak is yellow, and there are no specialized facial patches.  
Abdomen: Pale yellow with fine, inconspicuous barring; texture is soft and slightly downy.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a slight upcurved tip; primary feathers are dark brown with narrow white tips, and secondary feathers are pale yellow with dark margins.  
Tail: Short (approximately 50% of body length), conical in shape; upper tail coverts are black with a narrow pale yellow band at the base, while under tail coverts are pale yellow with fine black barring.  
Legs and Feet: Legs are slender and yellowish; feet are unwebbed with sharp, pointed claws (no webbing present).

Body Size: Medium-sized tern with a slender, streamlined body profile; overall length approximately 45–50 cm (excluding wings), slightly smaller than the Common Tern (*Sterna hirundo*) but more robust in build than juvenile forms. The body outline is aerodynamically efficient with a relatively narrow thorax and tapered hindquarters.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a pale grayish-brown upper body with fine, dark streaking along the back and scapulars; the underbody is pale gray with subtle buffish tints. Feather texture is dense with fine, interlocking vane structures typical of terns. Juveniles are uniformly duller brownish-gray with less defined streaking, softer plumage, and a more rounded body contour compared to adults.  
Beak: Long, slender, and sharply pointed with a dark gray to blackish base; tip is fine and slightly hooked for efficient prey capture. Length is approximately 50–55% of total body length, with minimal stoutness.  
Eyes: Dark brown irises.  
Face: Pale skin surrounding the eyes (periorbital area) with a distinct dark brown eye stripe; base of the beak is dark gray, and no prominent facial patches are present.  
Abdomen: Pale grayish-white with fine, irregular streaking of darker brownish-gray; texture is smooth and relatively soft.  
Wings: Long and narrow, with a pronounced curve; primary feathers are dark gray to black, and the wingtips are pale gray. The leading edge is dark, while the trailing edge shows subtle pale barring.  
Tail: Short, with a length of approximately 10–12 cm; shape is slightly rounded at the base and tapered. Upper tail coverts are dark gray, while under tail coverts are white with a pale grayish border.  
Legs and Feet: Dark gray to black coloration; feet are webbed (fully formed) with strong, sharp claws that are not hooked.

Body Size: Black Terns (Chlidonias niger) exhibit a compact, streamlined body size averaging 20–25 cm in length (excluding bill and legs), slightly smaller than the Common Tern (Hydroprogneites ardeola) but more robust than the Little Tern (Sternula niger). Their overall outline is characteristically slender with a relatively short neck and a distinctively deep, wedge-shaped chest, contrasting with the more elongated proportions of larger tern species.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a uniform slate-gray body plumage with a distinctive black cap and a pale, unmarked throat. Feather texture is smooth and slightly glossy, particularly on the head and upper body. Juveniles are duller, with brownish-gray head and neck, pale buff underparts, and less defined markings; they gradually acquire the adult's slate-gray hue and black cap over 1–2 years.  
Beak: The beak is dark grayish-black, moderately slender, and distinctly decurved (curved downward), with a sharp, pointed tip. It is relatively short for a tern, measuring approximately 15–18 mm in length, and lacks a pronounced hook.  
Eyes: The iris is a deep, uniform brown with no visible rings or variations.  
Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale grayish-white, bordered by a distinct dark eye stripe. The base of the beak is dark gray, and there are no prominent facial patches; the face is generally clean and unmarked compared to other terns.  
Abdomen: The abdomen is pale grayish-white with a faint yellowish sheen in adults; it is smooth and relatively short, lacking the pronounced white patches seen in some tern species.  
Wings: Wings are long and moderately pointed, with a dark grayish-brown coloration on the primary feathers and secondary coverts. The wingtips are pale gray, and the entire wing profile is relatively narrow for a tern.  
Tail: The tail is short (approximately 50–60% of body length), cylindrical in shape, and dark grayish-black. Upper tail coverts are uniformly black, while under tail coverts are pale grayish-white, creating a subtle contrast against the dark body.  
Legs and Feet: Legs are short and dark gray, with webbed feet typical of terns. The feet are moderately sized, and the claws are sharp and dark in color, adapted for aquatic foraging.

Body Size: The Caspian Tern (*Hydroprogne caspia*) exhibits a robust body size for a tern, measuring 55–65 cm in length (excluding bill and legs) with a wingspan of 120–140 cm. It is notably larger than the Common Tern (*Hydroprogne caspia*) and heavier than the Arctic Tern (*Sterna paradisaea*), with a streamlined, elongated body outline characteristic of large terns, featuring a relatively short neck and a distinctly tapered head.

Body Plumage: Adults display a dark brown to blackish upper body plumage with a pale, washed-out grayish-brown mantle, contrasting sharply with a pale, almost whitish underbody. The plumage is smooth, glossy, and densely packed with fine, stiff feathers. Juveniles are uniformly duller brown, with less defined contrasts, pale underparts, and a faintly streaked pattern on the flanks, gradually maturing to the adult plumage over 2–3 years.

Beak: The beak is long, slender, and sharply pointed, with a dark gray to blackish base and a distinct, sharp, black tip. It is moderately stout relative to the head size, measuring approximately 100–110% of the head length, and exhibits a slight downward curve at the tip, adapted for catching fish.

Eyes: The iris is uniformly dark brown, with no visible rings or distinct color variations.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eye) is pale grayish-white, forming a distinct pale stripe that extends from the base of the bill to the side of the head. The base of the beak is dark brown, contrasting with the pale periorbital region. There are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no bright markings or distinct color bands).

Abdomen: The abdomen is pale, washed-out grayish-white with a subtle yellowish tinge in adults, smooth and soft in texture, and lacks distinct barring or streaking. Juveniles have a more uniform pale brownish coloration.

Wings: The wings are long and narrow, with a pointed tip, and measure approximately 120–140 cm in length. The primary feathers are dark brown, while the secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown. The wingtips are white, and the coverts are pale, creating a distinct contrast against the darker body.

Tail: The tail is short (approximately 10–12 cm in length) and rounded at the tip. The upper tail coverts are dark brown, while the under tail coverts are pale grayish-white. The tail lacks distinct streaming or long feathers, maintaining a compact, functional structure for flight.

Legs and Feet: The legs are long, slender, and dark brown in color, with webbed feet (a characteristic adaptation for aquatic foraging). The feet are moderately large, with three functional toes (the fourth toe being reduced), and the claws are sharp and robust, suitable for gripping substrates while wading.

Body Size: Adult Common Terns (Sterna hirundo) exhibit a slender, elongated body structure measuring 30–35 cm in length (excluding wings), with a wingspan of 60–70 cm. This size places them slightly larger than the closely related Little Tern (Sterna albifrons) but notably smaller than the Arctic Tern (Sterna paradisaea), resulting in a relatively narrow, streamlined outline optimized for agile aerial maneuvers and rapid diving.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a distinct dark blue-black back and scapulars, contrasting with a pale, unmarked white underparts, including a conspicuous pale throat patch. Feather texture is smooth and slightly glossy, with fine, dense vane structure. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale streaking on the flanks and a duller, less defined pale throat, gradually transitioning to adult plumage over 2–3 years.  
Beak: The beak is slender, sharply pointed, and moderately long (30–35 mm), with a dark, almost black tip. It is relatively slender and not robust, reflecting the bird’s piscatorial feeding habits.  
Eyes: Iris color is uniformly dark brown.  
Face: The periorbital area (around the eye) is pale, with a distinct pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head. The base of the beak is dark, and there are no specialized facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: White in color, with a subtle yellowish tinge along the ventral margin. Texture is smooth and non-ribbed, typical of terns.  
Wings: Wings are long, narrow, and deeply pointed, with a dark brown leading edge and pale gray outer webs. The wingtips are rounded, and the overall shape is highly streamlined for efficient gliding and rapid takeoff.  
Tail: Tail length is 5–7 cm, short and relatively stiff. Upper tail coverts are dark brown, while under tail coverts are white, creating a clear contrast against the dark back.  
Legs and Feet: Legs are dark brown, slender, and moderately long. Feet are webbed (with three functional webbing zones), and claws are pointed and robust, adapted for gripping substrates during aquatic foraging.

Body Size: Medium-sized tern (45–50 cm total length), slightly smaller and more robust than the Common Tern (*Hydroprogne ruficollis*), with a streamlined, elongated body outline featuring a pointed head, narrow neck, and relatively short tail.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform dark slate-gray back and scapulars, contrasting with a pale, unmarked white underparts and a distinctive pale yellowish wash on the flanks. Feathers are smooth, glossy, and densely packed; juveniles display brownish streaking on the underparts and a duller, more variable grayish-brown upperparts with faint streaks along the flanks.  
Beak: Black, slender, and moderately curved with a sharp, pointed tip; upper beak slightly longer than lower beak, with a fine, delicate ridge along the base.  
Eyes: Pale yellow iris with a subtle golden sheen.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellowish-white with a distinct, narrow pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the side of the head; base of the beak is dark gray, with no specialized color patches or markings.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with a slight sheen, smooth texture, and minimal feathering; lacks distinct barring or streaking.  
Wings: Moderately long (25–30 cm), narrow and pointed with a slight curve; primary feathers dark blue-black with white tips, secondary feathers pale grayish-white, and a distinct white patch at the wingtip.  
Tail: Short (5–6 cm), rounded and slightly stiff; upper tail coverts dark brown, under tail coverts white with a pale yellowish edge.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown coloration, slender with webbed feet; toes are short, sharp, and equipped with strong, pointed claws (no webbing on the toes themselves).

Body Size: Forster's Tern (*Sterna forsteri*) measures 35–40 cm in length, exhibiting a slender, streamlined body typical of terns. It is slightly smaller than the Arctic Tern (*Sterna paradisaea*) but larger than the Common Tern (*Hydroprogne pratensis*), with a relatively short neck and a compact, aerodynamic outline that facilitates agile aerial foraging.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a dark grayish-brown upper body with pale grayish-white underparts, featuring fine, dense vane feathers. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with less defined contrast, pale underparts, and a faint streaking on the flanks; adults develop distinct blackish-brown upperparts and a prominent white throat patch absent in juveniles. Feather texture is smooth and slightly glossy, with minimal downy covering.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, slender and moderately long (approx. 45% of body length), with a sharply pointed tip that is slightly hooked (subterminal curvature) and no visible keratinous sheath.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white with a distinct, narrow white eye-ring; the base of the beak is dark gray, and there are no specialized facial patches beyond the eye-ring.  
Abdomen: Pale grayish-white with fine, dark brown streaking along the ventral surface, becoming less dense toward the base. Texture is smooth and non-iridescent.  
Wings: Long and narrow, with a wingspan of 75–85 cm; primary feathers are dark gray, secondary feathers pale gray, and the wingtips exhibit a subtle white margin. Wing shape is characteristically tern-like, with a high aspect ratio for efficient flight.  
Tail: Short (approx. 10 cm), rounded at the tip, with upper tail coverts dark gray and under tail coverts pale grayish-white. The tail lacks distinct white patches or markings.  
Legs and Feet: Dark gray coloration, slender and moderately long; feet are webbed (as in all terns) with three functional toes and a single, sharp claw on each toe.

Body Size: Approximately 18–20 cm in length (excluding wings), making it the smallest tern species globally. Significantly smaller than *Sterna* conspecifics (e.g., Common Tern *S. hirundo* at 25–30 cm) with a proportionally short, stubby neck and compact, streamlined body outline.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a pale grayish-brown upper body with a distinct pale brownish wash on the back and scapulars; plumage texture is smooth but slightly coarse. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with darker streaking on the flanks and a more pronounced pale rufous tinge on the crown, fading to pale gray in subsequent molts.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, short and slender (length ~25–30% of body), with a fine, slightly hooked tip and minimal curvature.  
Eyes: Iris is pale yellow.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale with a distinct pale yellowish stripe; base of the beak is dark gray, and no specialized facial patches or markings are present.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish with subtle olive undertones; texture is smooth and non-glossy.  
Wings: Short, narrow wings with a dark leading edge; color is pale gray to white, featuring a faint dark band along the wingtips and a white outer vane.  
Tail: Short, rounded, and relatively stiff; upper tail coverts are pale gray, while under tail coverts are white with minimal pigmentation.  
Legs and Feet: Dark gray to black in color, slender and relatively short; feet are moderately webbed with sharp, pointed claws.

Body Size: Approximately 18–20 cm in length, slightly smaller than the Eastern Towhee (*Pipilo erythrophthalmus*), with a compact, robust body outline and relatively short neck for a passerine.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform brownish-gray upper body with fine, dense vellus feathers; the central tail feathers are distinctly green (the namesake feature), while the rest of the body is pale brown with subtle grayish undertones. Juveniles display duller, more uniform brownish plumage with less defined green tail feathers and a lack of distinct barring, transitioning to adult plumage over 2–3 breeding seasons.  
Beak: Short, conical, and robust with a dark gray base and a slightly chisel-like tip; length is approximately 12 mm, with minimal curvature for terrestrial foraging.  
Eyes: Dark brown irises with a subtle golden sheen in optimal light.  
Face: Pale superciliary area (above the eye) with a distinct dark brown eye stripe; base of the beak is pale yellowish, contrasting with the darker facial skin.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with fine, irregular brown barring; texture is soft and slightly fluffy.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a slight upcurved tip; primary feathers are dark brown, while secondary feathers are pale gray with subtle white flight feather tips.  
Tail: Moderately long (approximately 100–120 mm), with the central tail feathers being vibrant green (most prominent in males); upper tail coverts are brownish-gray with fine blackish barring, and under tail coverts are pale yellow with subtle brownish edges.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender with sharp, pointed claws; feet are unwebbed and adapted for terrestrial movement on rocky terrain.

Body Size: Medium-large thrasher (25–28 cm in length), robust and stocky build with a relatively short neck compared to conspecifics like the Western Thrasher (*Toxostoma westi*). Overall outline is compact and slightly rounded, with a deep chest and broad base of the tail, contrasting with the more slender profiles of smaller thrasher species.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a complex, variable brownish-olive plumage (duller than *Toxostoma* species) with dense, fine-scale feathering; the upperparts are richly streaked with blackish-brown and pale brown, while the underparts are pale brown with fine blackish streaks. Juveniles are uniformly duller, with more extensive pale brown streaking on the flanks and a less defined pattern, and lack the distinct blackish markings of adults. Feather texture is dense, slightly coarse, and non-reflective.  
Beak: Dark brown to black, moderately long (approx. 18 mm), slender with a slightly curved tip, and robust at the base; the tip is sharp and slightly chisel-like, adapted for probing soil and vegetation.  
Eyes: Iris is uniformly dark brown.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale brown with a subtle, faintly stippled pattern; the base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no distinct facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: Pale brown with fine, irregular blackish-brown barring; texture is soft and slightly velvety.  
Wings: Moderately long (approx. 120 mm), broad and slightly rounded at the tip, with dark brown coverts and pale brown flight feathers; the primary feathers are dark brown with a pale brown tip.  
Tail: Long (approx. 100 mm), graduated with a distinct blackish-brown upper tail coverts and pale brown under tail coverts; the tail tip is pale brown with a subtle blackish-brown band.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown, sturdy, and slightly robust; feet are unwebbed with sharp, pointed claws (no webbing), typical of terrestrial birds.

Body Size: Medium-sized bird measuring 20–22 cm in length; slightly smaller than the Common Grackle (*Quiscalus quiscula*) but larger than the Western Meadowlark (*Sturnella neglecta*). Overall outline is compact with a moderately rounded breast and a relatively short, stubby neck, giving a slightly plump appearance compared to other thrasher species.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a grayish-brown upper body with subtle, fine streaking along the back and scapulars; underparts are pale grayish-brown with darker, irregular streaking concentrated on the flanks and ventral region. Feather texture is soft and slightly coarse, typical of thrashers. Juveniles are duller, with more uniform brownish-gray plumage, less defined streaking, and a paler underbelly compared to adults.  
Beak: Dark black in color, moderately long for body size, with a slightly hooked tip that is sharp but not excessively pointed; overall shape is robust and sturdy, consistent with seed-foraging adaptations.  
Eyes: Iris color is dark brown, with no visible distinct color variation.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-brown with a distinct pale stripe extending from the base of the bill to the eye; base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no white or contrasting markings).  
Abdomen: Pale grayish-brown with fine, irregular streaking of darker brown; texture is soft and non-velvety, with minimal downy covering.  
Wings: Medium length (approximately 15 cm), with a rounded, slightly tapered shape; primary feathers are dark brown, while secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown with subtle blackish tips. Flight feathers show minimal visible contrast against the body.  
Tail: Relatively short (about 7 cm), with a rounded tip; upper tail coverts are dark brown, and under tail coverts are pale grayish-brown with fine streaking. Tail shape is moderately stiff but not rigid.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with strong, pointed claws; feet are non-webbed, typical of terrestrial birds, and adapted for walking on ground rather than swimming.

Body Size: Compact and streamlined with a body length of 12–13 cm; slightly smaller than the Yellow-throated Vireo (*Vireo flavifrons*) and more robust than the Black-throated Green Vireo (*Vireo solitarius*), exhibiting a characteristic warbler-like body outline with a relatively short neck and narrow thorax.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a uniform black cap, olive-green upperparts with fine, dense vireo-type feathers, and a bright yellow throat patch; the plumage is smooth and non-reflective with subtle olive-green streaking on the flanks. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray above with pale yellowish-brown underparts, lacking the distinct black cap and bright throat patch, and exhibit duller, less densely packed feathers with a more variable olive-brown hue.  
Beak: Dark grayish-brown in color, slender, moderately pointed, and slightly curved at the tip; length is approximately 10 mm, with a fine, sharp tip adapted for insect manipulation.  
Eyes: Iris is a pale yellowish-white in adults, fading to a duller yellow in juveniles.  
Face: Periorbital area features a distinct pale supercilium (white stripe) above the eye, a narrow pale eye-ring, and a dark eye stripe; base of the beak is pale yellowish, with no specialized facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: White with faint, fine olive-green streaking; texture is smooth and non-glossy, lacking any distinct patterning.  
Wings: Moderately long (approx. 65 mm), narrow and pointed with a slight curve at the tip; leading edge is pale grayish-white, trailing edge is darker brown, and the wing coverts are uniformly pale with subtle brownish tints.  
Tail: Short (approx. 40 mm), rounded and slightly flattened; upper tail coverts are dark brown, while under tail coverts are white with a pale yellowish base; tail feathers are short and stiff, lacking prominent central tail feathers.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender and relatively short; feet are unwebbed with sharp, pointed claws, typical of terrestrial insectivores.

Body Size: 14–15 cm in length (excluding tail), with a compact, slightly rounded body outline. Slightly smaller than the Yellow-throated Vireo (*Vireo flavifrons*) and more robust than the Black-throated Green Vireo (*Vireo solitarius*); overall proportions are slender with a relatively short neck and short tail, typical of the vireo family.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a vivid cerulean blue head (intensifying to near-black in direct sunlight on the crown), contrasting sharply with a pale yellow throat and a pale olive-brown body. Feather texture is smooth, glossy, and fine, with subtle iridescence on the head. Juveniles are duller, with olive-brown heads, pale buff underparts, and a faint, non-reflective blue sheen on the crown; they lack the intense cerulean of adults and show no distinct throat patch.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved; length 10–12 mm. Color is black with a fine, sharp tip; base is dark brown. No webbing, consistent with insectivorous feeding habits.  
Eyes: Iris color is dark brown (not green or yellow), with a subtle pale yellowish hue around the pupil in natural light.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellow, with a distinct pale superciliary arch (eyebrow ridge) that transitions smoothly into the cerulean head plumage. Base of the beak is dark brown, matching the head plumage; no specialized facial patches (e.g., streaks or spots) are present.  
Abdomen: White with a faint yellowish tinge, soft and fluffy texture; no streaking or barring.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings (typical of vireos); length 80–90% of body length. Primary feathers are dark brown, secondaries pale brown, with a subtle pale buff color on the trailing edge. Wing profile is relatively stiff and compact.  
Tail: Length 100–120 mm; short, rounded, and slightly flattened. Upper tail coverts are dark brown with a pale buff border; under tail coverts are pale brown with minimal contrast. Tail feathers are short and stiff, lacking the long, graduated shape seen in some other vireos.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender and relatively short; feet are unwebbed with sharp, pointed claws (no webbing), adapted for perching on small twigs and foraging on the ground.

Body Size: Philadelphia Vireo (Vireo philadelphius) measures 14–15 cm in length with a wingspan of 20–22 cm. It exhibits a compact, rounded body outline with a relatively short tail (approx. 50% of body length), slightly smaller than the Western Vireo (Vireo gilvus) but comparable in size to the Yellow-throated Vireo (Vireo flavifrons). The overall silhouette is slender with a distinctively short, stubby neck.

Body Plumage: Adults display a uniform, pale olive-green upper body with a subtle, fine-scale texture. The underparts are pale yellowish-white, transitioning to a more washed-out yellow on the flanks. Juveniles are distinctly duller, with a brownish-olive back, pale grayish-brown underparts, and a less pronounced yellow throat patch. The plumage is non-iridescent and relatively smooth, lacking the pronounced gloss of some other vireo species. Adults show minimal seasonal variation.

Beak: Short, stout, and slightly decurved, with a dark grayish-black coloration. The beak tip is blunt and slightly chisel-like, consistent with its insectivorous diet. The beak length is approximately 12–14 mm, proportionally short relative to head size.

Eyes: Dark brown irises, with no visible scleral ring or distinct color variation.

Face: Features a pale, narrow superciliary arch (eyebrow) and a distinct pale yellowish-white throat patch that extends posteriorly to the base of the neck. The base of the beak is dark grayish-brown, and there are no prominent white or black facial patches distinguishing it from other vireos.

Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with a faint, subtle yellowish tinge along the edges. The texture is soft and downy, with minimal visible feathering.

Wings: Moderately short and rounded, with a slight upcurved tip. Primary feathers are dark brown, while secondary feathers are olive-green. The wing pattern is relatively uniform, lacking the distinct pale coverts seen in some vireo species.

Tail: Relatively short (approx. 40–45 mm), with a graduated, slightly flattened shape. Upper tail coverts are dark brown, and under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white. The tail exhibits minimal visible feathering at the base.

Legs and Feet: Dark grayish-brown in color, slender with sharp, pointed claws. Feet are non-webbed, typical of terrestrial songbirds, and adapted for perching on small branches.

Body Size: Medium-sized songbird measuring 10–11 cm in length; slender and relatively compact compared to larger vireo species (e.g., Common Grackle), with a distinctly curved body outline and a proportionally short neck.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a clean, uniform black upperparts (including crown, nape, and mantle) with a sharply defined white underparts (ventral region), lacking streaking or spotting. Feather texture is smooth and glossy; juveniles display duller, brownish-gray upperparts and pale buff underparts with subtle, faint streaking along the flanks, fading to near-adult plumage by the second year.  
Beak: Short, stout, and slightly decurved (not hooked), with a dark gray-black coloration; tip is blunt and slightly chisel-like, consistent with its insectivorous diet.  
Eyes: Iris is a vivid, unchanging crimson red (not reddish-brown), a defining characteristic of the species.  
Face: Periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale grayish-white with a distinct, narrow red eye patch extending posteriorly from the orbital region; base of the beak is dark gray-black, with no additional facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: Uniformly white with fine, soft texture; no barring, streaking, or variation in coloration.  
Wings: Moderately long (span ~15 cm), with pointed tips and a slight curve; primary feathers are dark gray-black, secondary feathers are pale gray, and the wing coverts are black.  
Tail: Short (length ~4 cm), rounded and slightly flattened; upper tail coverts are black, while under tail coverts are white with a subtle, narrow black band at the base.  
Legs and Feet: Short, dark gray-black in color; feet are unwebbed with sharp, pointed claws (adapted for perching on twigs), typical of arboreal songbirds.

Body Size: Approximately 10–11 cm in length, with a compact, somewhat rounded body outline. Slightly smaller than the Yellow-throated Vireo (*Vireo flavifrons*) but comparable in size to the Common Yellowthroat (*Geothlypis trichas*); overall proportions are slender with a relatively short neck and short tail, typical of vireos.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a bright, iridescent green upper body (including head and back) with a pale yellow throat patch and a distinct pale yellowish-brownish supercilium. Feathers are smooth, glossy, and densely packed, with minimal downy covering. Juveniles display a duller olive-brown upper body, pale grayish-brown throat, and a less defined pale stripe across the face, lacking the vivid green and yellow of adults; plumage becomes progressively brighter and more defined over 2–3 breeding seasons.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly curved at the tip; color is dark grayish-black with a fine, sharp apex. Length is approximately 12–15 mm, and the beak is relatively delicate and not stout, adapted for precise insect manipulation.  
Eyes: Iris color is dark brown, with minimal visible variation between individuals.  
Face: Periorbital area (around the eye) is pale yellowish-brown, forming a distinct pale stripe from the base of the bill to the side of the head; base of the beak is dark grayish-black, and there are no specialized facial patches beyond the pale periorbital stripe and the yellow throat patch.  
Abdomen: Pale yellow to whitish coloration with a fine, soft texture; no streaking or barring present.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a slight upcurved tip; flight feathers (remiges) are pale gray with dark brownish tips, and the coverts are pale gray. Wing length is approximately 60–70 mm, relatively short for the body size.  
Tail: Medium length (approximately 50–60 mm), with a graduated shape (broad base tapering to a pointed tip); upper tail coverts are pale greenish-yellow, while under tail coverts are pale yellow. Tail feathers are relatively stiff and show minimal plumage variation.  
Legs and Feet: Dark gray coloration, slender and relatively short; feet are non-webbed with sharp, pointed claws, typical of insectivorous birds.

Body Size: Approximately 12–14 cm in length, with a compact, somewhat rounded body outline. Slightly smaller than the closely related Yellow-throated Vireo (*Vireo flavifrons*) and proportionally more slender than the Black-capped Vireo (*Vireo atacama*), exhibiting a relatively short neck and short tail relative to body mass.

Body Plumage: Adults display a predominantly olive-green upper body with pale grayish underparts. Feather texture is fine, soft, and slightly glossy. Juveniles are duller, with brownish-gray upperparts and pale buff underparts, lacking the distinct white eye-ring and showing less defined plumage patterns; adult plumage becomes sharply defined with a contrasting white eye-ring by the second breeding season.

Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved, measuring 10–12 mm in length. Tip is blackish with a fine, sharp point; base is pale gray, consistent with vireo family morphology.

Eyes: Iris is a uniform yellowish-green, lacking distinct color variation or spotting.

Face: Periorbital area features a narrow, conspicuous white eye-ring (a defining characteristic) that contrasts sharply with the dark facial skin. Base of the beak is pale gray, with no distinct facial patches or markings.

Abdomen: Pale grayish-white in color, with a soft, fine texture and minimal visible down. Slightly paler than the ventral underparts.

Wings: Moderately short and rounded, with a length of approximately 60–70% of body length. Primary feathers are pale gray, and secondary coverts are faintly brownish-gray; overall wing coloration is pale gray with subtle brownish tones on the coverts.

Tail: Medium length (approximately 50% of body length), with a graduated shape. Upper tail coverts are pale gray, and under tail coverts are pale white. Tail tip is slightly rounded, with no prominent central tail feathers.

Body Size: Approximately 14–15 cm in length, with a slender, elongated body profile. Slightly smaller and more compact than the Common Vireo (*Vireo olivaceus*) but comparable in overall proportions to the Black-throated Vireo (*Vireo atricollis*); the head is relatively large for its body size, giving a delicate, agile appearance with minimal body mass.

Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a distinct yellow throat and upper chest (ventral region) contrasting with a pale olive-green back and rump. The underparts are grayish-brown with fine, soft feather texture; the plumage is uniformly dense with short, fine vireo-type feathers. Juveniles display duller, more uniform grayish-brown plumage across the body, with a faint, pale yellowish tinge on the throat and minimal contrast between upper and lower parts, lacking the vivid yellow of adults.

Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved at the tip; length measures 10–12 mm. Color is dark gray to black, with a sharp, pointed tip that is not chisel-like. The beak is relatively robust for its size but lacks the pronounced curvature seen in some other vireo species.

Eyes: Iris color is dark brown, uniformly shaded without variation.

Face: Periorbital area (around the eye) is pale grayish-brown, blending smoothly into the base of the beak, which is dark gray. No distinct facial patches, markings, or rufous tones are present; the face is clean and unadorned.

Abdomen: Pale yellow to cream-colored, with a smooth, non-ribbed texture. Juveniles show a more uniform grayish-brown abdomen with less pronounced yellowing.

Wings: Moderately long (approximately 60–70 mm), with pointed tips and a slight tapering. Coloration is grayish-brown on the upper surfaces, transitioning to pale white on the flight feathers (remiges), with a subtle, faintly visible pale band along the leading edge.

Tail: Short, rounded in shape, and relatively stiff. Upper tail coverts are grayish-brown with fine, dark barring; under tail coverts are pale yellow, slightly shorter than the upper tail coverts, and lack distinct feathering.

Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender and relatively short for their body size. Feet are unwebbed, with sharp, pointed claws suitable for perching on small branches; no visible pads or specialized structures.

Body Size: 14–16 cm in length, slender build with a moderately elongated neck; slightly smaller than the Yellow-rumped Warbler (13–15 cm) but larger than the Yellow Warbler (12–14 cm); overall outline is elongated and streamlined with a subtle tapering from the head to the tail.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a distinctive "bay" coloration on the upperparts (olive-brown to dark brown) with a pale yellowish throat and a narrow, pale superciliary arch; juveniles are uniformly duller, with pale grayish-brown upperparts, faint streaking on the flanks, and a pale buff throat. Feather texture is fine and soft with a slight gloss to the vane edges; the plumage is relatively dense but not heavily barred.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, slender and moderately decurved, with a fine, sharp tip; length approximately 12–15 mm, slightly shorter than the Yellow Warbler’s beak.  
Eyes: Iris is a pale yellowish-brown in adults, less vivid than the Yellow-rumped Warbler’s but distinctly visible against the pale face.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellowish-brown with a narrow, distinct pale superciliary arch; base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no eye-rings or streaks).  
Abdomen: White with faint, fine brownish streaks in males during breeding season; females show a more uniform pale brownish-gray coloration. Texture is smooth and unmarked.  
Wings: Moderately long (100–110 mm), pointed tips with a slight curve; primary feathers are dark brown, secondary coverts are pale yellowish-brown, and the wing coverts display subtle barring.  
Tail: Short (approximately 50% of body length), graduated in shape; upper tail coverts are dark brown with pale edges, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-brown with faint, fine streaking.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender with sharp, pointed claws; feet are unwebbed, typical of terrestrial warblers.

Body Size: Small passerine measuring 10–11 cm in length; slightly smaller than Yellow-rumped Warbler (*Setophaga coronata*) but comparable in size to Yellow-throated Warbler (*Setophaga coronata*). Compact body outline with a relatively short neck and tapered tail, exhibiting a streamlined yet robust build typical of understory warblers.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a striking black-and-white pattern: dark grayish-black upperparts with fine, dense blackish-brown streaking on the mantle and scapulars, contrasting sharply with a pale white underparts featuring distinct blackish-brown streaks from the throat to the flanks. Juveniles are duller, with overall brownish-gray upperparts, faint streaking, and pale buff underparts lacking the sharp black streaks of adults; plumage becomes progressively more defined and black-and-white as they mature. Feather texture is fine and dense, with subtle gloss in the black areas.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved; dark brownish-black in color, with a fine, sharp tip and minimal curvature. Length is approximately 10–12 mm, consistent with small warblers.  
Eyes: Iris is dark brown, with a uniform hue lacking prominent color variation.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white with a distinct, narrow pale stripe extending from the eye to the base of the bill; base of the beak is dark brownish-black, and no specialized facial patches (e.g., white or black) are present.  
Abdomen: Pale white with fine, dense blackish-brown streaking; texture is smooth and non-velvety, with minimal visible down.  
Wings: Short, rounded wings with a slight upcurved tip; upperwing coverts are dark brownish-black, while flight feathers (remiges) are pale grayish-white with blackish-brown tips. Wing length is approximately 50–55 mm.  
Tail: Medium length (approximately 50–55 mm), graduated with a slightly flattened tip; upper tail coverts are uniformly black, while under tail coverts are pale white with fine blackish-brown streaking.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, slender with sharp, pointed claws; feet are non-webbed, typical of terrestrial warblers, and adapted for perching on twigs.

Body Size: Medium-sized warbler (12–13 cm in length), slightly smaller than the Black-throated Green Warbler conspecific. Exhibits a slender, elongated body outline with a relatively short neck and tapered tail, typical of the *Setophaga* genus; juveniles are 10–11% smaller with less defined proportions.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a striking, intense cobalt-blue upperparts (mantle, back, and rump) with a narrow, sharply defined black throat patch (1.5–2.0 cm wide) contrasting sharply with the rest of the plumage. Feather texture is fine vellus to smooth shafts, with subtle iridescence under direct light. Juveniles are uniformly olive-brown with pale buff underparts, no black throat patch, and duller blue hues on the upperparts; they lack the vivid contrast of adults and show minimal structural coloration.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved (curvature ~15°), with a dark grayish-black base and a fine, sharp tip (no pronounced hook). Length is approximately 12 mm, consistent with other *Setophaga* warblers but proportionally more delicate.  
Eyes: Bright yellow iris with a pale yellowish-white central region.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellowish-white with no streaking or barring; base of the beak is dark grayish-black, contrasting with the pale face. No distinct facial patches or markings beyond the black throat.  
Abdomen: White with a faint, diffuse brownish-tint (especially in the central region), smooth and unfeathered texture.  
Wings: Moderately short (span ~10 cm), rounded and slightly stiff in profile; primary feathers are dark grayish-brown with subtle blue edges, while secondary feathers are pale blue. Wing coverts are dark brown with narrow blue margins.  
Tail: Long (approximately 50% of body length), graduated with a distinct blackish-brown upper tail coverts (1.5–2.0 cm wide) exhibiting a narrow, pale blue band along the outer margin; under tail coverts are white with faint blue tinge.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brownish-black in color, slender with sharp, pointed claws (non-webbed). Foot structure is typical of terrestrial warblers, with a short tarsus and reduced digit length.

Body Size: 12–14 cm in length, with a slender, elongated body profile that is slightly shorter and more compact than the closely related Yellow Warbler (*Setophaga petrosa*). The overall outline is distinctly wedge-shaped with a moderately deep chest and a relatively short neck, typical of parulid warblers.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a finely streaked olive-brown upperparts with pale brownish-grayish streaking on the flanks, contrasting with a white underbody and pale yellowish throat. The plumage is soft and dense, with fine, short feathers that lack prominent gloss. Juveniles are duller, showing more extensive brownish streaking on the upperparts and a less defined white underbody with faint brownish tints, lacking the distinct blue wing patches of adults.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved (not hooked), with a dark brown base and a pale yellowish tip. The beak is relatively robust for its size but not stout, measuring approximately 10–12 mm in length.  
Eyes: Iris color is a uniform yellowish-brown, lacking distinct rings or patterns.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale yellowish with a narrow, dark brown eye stripe extending from the base of the bill. The base of the beak is pale yellow, and there are no specialized facial patches (e.g., no white or black markings) distinguishing this species from conspecifics.  
Abdomen: White with fine, pale brownish streaking along the ventral side, texture is smooth and non-glossy, with minimal visible feathering.  
Wings: Moderately short for the body length (approximately 60–70% of total body length), narrow and pointed with dark brown upper coverts. The wings are characterized by a distinct, narrow blue patch on the greater coverts and a pale blue band on the secondary coverts visible only in flight, contrasting with the brownish primaries and secondaries.  
Tail: Relatively long (approximately 50% of body length), graduated with a stiff, slightly curved shape. Upper tail coverts are dark brown with subtle pale barring, while under tail co:verts are white with faint brownish edges. The tail is not fluffy but maintains a rigid, angular structure typical of warblers.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with sharp, pointed claws and non-webbed feet (adapted for perching on twigs). The tarsus (leg) is short and robust relative to the body size.

Body Size: 14–15 cm in length, smaller than congenerics such as the Yellow Warbler (*Setophaga petrosa*) and the Yellow-rumped Warbler (*Setophaga coronata*); compact, laterally compressed body with a relatively short neck and slender proportions, giving an overall streamlined outline typical of wood-warblers.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a uniform olive-brown upperparts with subtle, fine-scale variation in hue (darker on the back, paler on the mantle); ventral plumage is pale yellow with distinct, fine dark brown barring on the flanks and breast; feather texture is soft and slightly glossy, with a dense, short vane structure. Juveniles are duller, with more extensive brownish tones on the upperparts and less pronounced barring, lacking the bright yellow throat patch of adults.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, slender and moderately decurved, measuring 10–12 mm in length; tip is sharp and slightly chisel-like, with minimal keratinized sheath.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris.  
Face: Pale yellowish superciliary arch (above the eye), contrasting with a dark brown eye stripe; base of the beak is pale yellow, with a distinct, narrow yellowish patch extending posteriorly from the eye region.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with fine, irregular dark brown barring; texture is soft and slightly fluffy, lacking prominent gloss.  
Wings: Short, measuring 50–60 mm in length; shape is rounded with a slight taper, featuring dark brown upperwing coverts and a pale yellowish-brown secondary coverts; primary feathers are relatively short and stiff.  
Tail: Short, measuring 40–50 mm in length; shape is graduated with a slightly flattened tip; upper tail coverts are pale yellow with distinct white tips on the outermost feathers; under tail coverts are pale yellow with minimal barring.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color; feet are short and robust with sharp, pointed claws (non-webbed), typical of terrestrial foragers.

Body Size: 12–13 cm in length, with a compact, streamlined body proportionate to its size. Slightly smaller than the Yellow-rumped Warbler (*Setophaga coronata*) but comparable in overall outline to the Yellow Warbler (*Setophaga petrosa*); the head is relatively large for its body size, contributing to a distinctive, alert appearance.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a finely textured, slightly glossy olive-brown back with a subtle olive wash on the flanks, contrasting sharply with a pale yellowish-white throat and upper breast. The underparts are pale yellow with a faint, irregular olive-brown streaking on the flanks and a distinct, narrow yellowish band across the chest. Juveniles are duller, with a more uniform brownish-gray back, pale buff underparts, and a less defined yellowish throat patch, lacking the adult’s distinct olive wash and streaking.  
Beak: Slender, moderately curved, 10–12 mm in length, with a slightly hooked tip adapted for insect manipulation; the base is robust but tapers gradually to the tip.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris.  
Face: Features a pale, narrow superciliary arch (eyebrow) contrasting with the dark brown eye region; the base of the beak is pale yellowish, and a distinct, narrow yellowish patch extends from the eye posteriorly along the cheek to the throat.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white, with fine, short feathers creating a soft, slightly textured appearance; no distinct barring or streaking.  
Wings: Moderately short (approximately 60–70% of body length), with a rounded tip; the primary feathers are dark brown, the secondary feathers are pale olive-brown, and the coverts are uniformly dark brown with subtle pale edges.  
Tail: Short (approximately 30–40% of body length), with an upright, slightly graduated shape; upper tail coverts are olive-brown with pale edges, while under tail coverts are pale yellowish-white with fine, short feathers.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with sharp, pointed claws; feet are non-webbed, typical of warblers, and adapted for perching on twigs.

Body Size: Approximately 12–13 cm in length, with a slender, elongated body typical of warblers. Slightly smaller and more delicate than the Yellow Warbler (*Setophaga petrosa*) and less robust than the Black-throated Blue Warbler (*Setophaga caerulescens*), exhibiting a streamlined, tapered outline with a relatively short neck and narrow chest.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a striking iridescent blue upper body (crown, nape, and mantle) that transitions to a pale olive-green on the flanks and ventral regions. Feathers are fine, slightly glossy, and densely packed, with subtle barring on the flanks. Juveniles are duller, featuring a brownish-olive mantle, pale yellowish-brown underparts, and a lack of iridescence, with plumage gradually developing adult coloration over 2–3 years.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved (curved downward at the tip), measuring approximately 8–9 mm in length. Color is dark grayish-black with a fine, sharp tip that is not distinctly hooked.  
Eyes: Iris is a vivid, uniform yellow.  
Face: Features a pale, narrow supercilium (eyebrow stripe) above the eye, a distinct dark eye stripe, and a pale, unmarked region between the eye and base of the beak. No prominent facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: Pale yellowish-white with fine, irregular brownish barring. Texture is soft and slightly fluffy.  
Wings: Moderately short (approximately 60% of body length), with a narrow, pointed shape. Primary feathers are dark brown, while secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown with subtle white tips. Wing coverts are dark brown with faint pale edges.  
Tail: Relatively short (about 40% of body length), with a slightly graduated shape. Upper tail coverts are deep blue (iridescent) and narrowly edged with white. Under tail coverts are white with faint brownish streaking.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown in color, with short, strong, sharp claws (non-webbed). Feet are adapted for perching and terrestrial movement on vegetation.

Body Size: 12–13 cm in length, slender and relatively compact with a slightly curved body outline; notably smaller than the Yellow-throated Warbler (14–15 cm) but comparable in size to the Yellow Warbler (12–14 cm), with a proportionally short neck and fine-tipped tail.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a distinct chestnut patch on the central breast, contrasting with pale olive-brown upperparts and white underparts; feather texture is fine, soft, and slightly glossy; juveniles are uniformly olive-brown with duller, less defined chestnut patches and lack the prominent white underparts of adults, appearing more uniformly brownish.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly decurved; color is dark grayish-brown with a pale base; tip is blunt, not hooked.  
Eyes: Iris is pale yellow.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale buff with a subtle yellowish tint; base of the beak is dark grayish-brown; no distinct facial patches or markings.  
Abdomen: White with a faint yellowish tinge; texture is smooth and non-reflective.  
Wings: Medium length (approx. 65–70% of body length), narrow with pointed tips; coloration includes pale grayish-brown on the leading edge and olive-brown on the trailing edge, with a distinct pale central patch on the remex.  
Tail: Relatively short (approx. 40% of body length), graduated; upper tail coverts are pale brown with subtle olive undertones, while under tail coverts are white with a faint pale brown border.  
Legs and Feet: Dark brown; slender with sharp, pointed claws; feet are unwebbed and adapted for terrestrial movement.

Body Size: Small passerine measuring 12–15 cm in length, with a compact, streamlined body typical of warblers. Slightly smaller than the Yellow-throated Warbler (*Setophaga xanthogastris*) but comparable in size to the Black-throated Green Warbler (*Dendroica virens*), exhibiting a proportionally robust thorax and slender hindlimb structure.  
Body Plumage: Adults display a striking golden-yellow patch on the central pair of scapulars (wing coverts), contrasting with a pale olive-green back and a brownish head. Underparts are pale yellow with fine, inconspicuous barring. Juveniles exhibit duller plumage, with less intense golden tones, a more uniform brownish hue across the body, and reduced barring on the underparts.  
Beak: Short, slender, and slightly curved, with a black coloration and a fine, sharp tip.  
Eyes: Dark brown iris.  
Face: Pale skin surrounding the eyes, with no distinct periorbital patches; the base of the beak is dark brown.  
Abdomen: Pale yellow with faint, fine barring.  
Wings: Short and pointed, with the central pair of scapulars (wing coverts) displaying the characteristic golden-yellow coloration.  
Tail: Moderately long (approx. 50% of body length), with a graduated shape; upper tail coverts are black with white tips, and under tail coverts are pale yellow.  
Legs and Feet: Short, dark brown, with sharp claws; feet are not webbed.
